title: Bengals progress report: Grading special teams
summary: The Cincinnati Bengals are 3-2 coming out of their bye week, and depending on which side of the bed you wake up on, there’s plenty of reason for optimism or pessimism. The offense has had its moments. The defense has had its moments. Unfortunately, so have the special teams, and not necessarily in a good […]
full_text: The Cincinnati Bengals are 3-2 coming out of their bye week, and depending on which side of the bed you wake up on, there’s plenty of reason for optimism or pessimism. The offense has had its moments. The defense has had its moments. Unfortunately, so have the special teams, and not necessarily in a good way. Outside of Evan McPherson, who apparently decided missing field goals is for lesser mortals, Darrin Simmons’ special teams units have been a frustrating combination of mediocrity and outright disaster. Let’s start with the one guy who’s been keeping the lights on. Field Goal/Field Goal Block With 11 guys on the field working together, every play has a lot of moving pieces, but the field-goal unit is fairly simple. As long as the long snapper, holder, and kicker do their jobs, everyone else just needs to keep the defense out of the way for a second or two. Outside of a penalty that pushed the Bengals out of field-goal range, Evan McPherson and the rest of the field-goal unit have been perfect. McPherson now owns the franchise record for most consecutive field goals made with 22, a streak that stretches back to the 2025 season. In 2026, McPherson is a perfect 10-for-10. What’s most impressive, though, is that five of those kicks have come from 50 or more yards, with a long of 58. Obviously, the offense wants to walk away from every drive with seven points, but that’s not always possible. The Bengals are extremely fortunate to have a kicker who is so accurate from beyond 50 yards. Nobody really cares about the kicker until a field goal can win or lose the game in the final minutes. On the defensive side of things, the only major issue so far this season came in Week 5. Dexter Lawrence was flagged for roughing the snapper against the Dolphins, giving Miami a fresh set of downs after a successful field goal. The Dolphins eventually scored a touchdown, turning three points into seven. The Bengals won that game, but those four additional points helped keep Miami within striking distance late in the fourth quarter. Field Goal Unit: 98% (A+) Field Goal Block Unit: 85% (B) Overall Field Goal Unit: 92% (A-) Punt/Punt Return Here’s where the real problems begin. As far as punt coverage goes, the first major mistake came in Week 3 against the Steelers. The Bengals’ defense stopped Pittsburgh in the third quarter and forced a punt, but Cedric Johnson was called for an obvious roughing-the-kicker penalty. That gave the Steelers a fresh set of downs, and what should have been a defensive stop turned into a Pittsburgh touchdown a few plays later. In the same game, former punt returner Ke’Shawn Williams muffed a punt that Pittsburgh recovered at the Bengals’ 14-yard line. The defense managed to hold the Steelers to a field goal, but instead of Cincinnati getting the ball back with an opportunity to score, Pittsburgh walked away with three points. Those two mistakes handed the Steelers possessions that resulted in 10 points in a game the Bengals lost by three. Ryan Rehkow’s punting, meanwhile, has been unspectacular. His 44.9 yards-per-punt average ranks among the lowest in the NFL. Nine of his 16 punts have been downed inside the 20-yard line, and he hasn’t recorded a touchback. There haven’t been any major mistakes on Rehkow’s part, but his overall production has been below average. The real issue with this unit isn’t necessarily the punter. It’s the mistakes being made around him. A roughing penalty and a muffed punt aren’t just bad plays. They’re the kinds of mistakes that can cost a team a game, and against Pittsburgh, they helped do exactly that. Punting Unit: 74% (C) Punt Return Unit: 49% (F) Overall Punting grade: 61 (D-) Kickoff/Kickoff Return Kickoffs are so different now than they used to be. With touchbacks generally bringing the ball out to the 35-yard line, teams have more incentive to kick short of the end zone and force a return. That means more opportunities for explosive plays, but it also means more opportunities for mistakes. For the Bengals, the most glaring mistake came in Week 5 against the Dolphins. Rookie wide receiver Dohnte Meyers fielded a kickoff at the four-yard line, but his momentum carried him out of bounds almost immediately, setting Joe Burrow and the offense up in the shadow of their own goalposts. The offense managed to move the ball out near midfield, but the drive ultimately ended with a punt. While the mistake didn’t directly cost Cincinnati points, it put the offense in a difficult position and eliminated any chance of starting that possession with favorable field position. To be fair, Meyers also started that game with an 81-yard kickoff return that set the Bengals up at Miami’s 10-yard line. Burrow and the offense took advantage, scoring a touchdown just three plays later. That’s the frustrating thing about the kickoff return unit. There’s clearly potential for big plays, but the execution hasn’t always been consistent. On the coverage side, the Bengals haven’t suffered any major breakdowns comparable to what we’ve seen from the punt units. They’ve generally done a respectable job of limiting opposing returners and avoiding the kind of disastrous plays that can completely flip field position. Kickoff Unit Grade: 82% (B-) Kickoff Return Unit Grade: 79% (C+) Overall Kickoff/Return Grade: 80% (B -) Darrin Simmons has been the Bengals’ special teams coordinator since 2003. He was named assistant head coach in 2020 and has held both positions ever since. Special teams typically haven’t been a major problem for the Bengals under Simmons, but this season has been different. Outside of McPherson, the unit has made several costly mistakes, and some have had a direct impact on the outcome of games. Look no further than Pittsburgh. The Bengals lost that game by three points, and two special teams mistakes gave the Steelers possessions that resulted in 10 points. It’s impossible to say with certainty how the game would have unfolded without those errors, but it’s hard not to wonder what Cincinnati’s record would look like if those mistakes hadn’t happened. It’s not all on Simmons. Players have to execute, and there are only so many things a coach can control once the ball is snapped. However, Simmons is responsible for preparing his units, and right now, those units aren’t consistently getting the job done. A 4-1 record, including a 1-0 start in the division, would sound a hell of a lot better than 3-2. Hopefully, the Bengals got things straightened out during the bye week. Because without McPherson’s excellence, Cincinnati’s special teams would be earning a solid D. Overall Special Teams Grade: 77% C

Casey can see All making a huge catch like Hudson did last week, when he mowed the grass with his hands to scoop up a third-and-seven conversion that kept a drive going where he scored a touchdown.” The Bengals used their bye to look inward. Here’s what stood out “Taylor said the staff used the week to evaluate the team and prepare for the schedule ahead. For the players, the pause also offered time to recover and continue working back from injuries. The broader goal, Taylor said, is to turn promising stretches into a more consistent performance across the entire roster.”

title: DJ Turner is having a good season, even if you’re not noticing it
summary: A sign of a great cornerback is if you don’t notice him. It sounds weird, but if you don’t notice him, it means that the opposing quarterback isn’t throwing in his direction. Bengals cornerback DJ Turner hasn’t been noticed in most of the Bengals’ first five games this season. The only time he really has […]
full_text: A sign of a great cornerback is if you don’t notice him. It sounds weird, but if you don’t notice him, it means that the opposing quarterback isn’t throwing in his direction. Bengals cornerback DJ Turner hasn’t been noticed in most of the Bengals’ first five games this season. The only time he really has was when he drew a holding call against DK Metcalf late in the game at the Steelers in Week 3. Turner hasn’t let potential distractions regarding a contract extension impact him, and that goes all the way back to this offseason. The proof has been in his play so far this season. Bengals CB DJ Turner is making a strong case to be a potential All-Pro corner this year. Has been very sticky in coverage and surrendered very few yards per coverage snap. (also: MY WORD, Trent McDuffie!!) pic.twitter.com/fMd5xS6B8l — Ben Baby (@Ben_Baby) October 14, 2026 For those in the analytics crowd, this is for you. Admittedly, I’m not an analytics guy. But this illustrates the season Turner is having through five games. He’s allowing barely a half-yard per coverage snap, which is impressive. Turner has five passes defensed this season and 12 tackles. Impressively, nine of those are solo tackles.

title: Browns: Quarterback D-Day is looming on the horizon
summary: The narrative around the Cleveland Browns’ starting quarterback has evolved since the season opened. From what was once “Deshaun Watson will be benched by the home opener,” it transitioned to “Will he be the starter next week,” then to “Watson’s runway has gotten longer,” to the current “Watson is going to be the starting quarterback […]
full_text: (Photo by Frank Jansky/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The narrative around the Cleveland Browns’ starting quarterback has evolved since the season opened. From what was once “Deshaun Watson will be benched by the home opener,” it transitioned to “Will he be the starter next week,” then to “Watson’s runway has gotten longer,” to the current “Watson is going to be the starting quarterback the rest of the season, unless he gets injured.” Winning cures many things in the NFL, and nowhere is that truer than in Cleveland, where the Browns are first in the AFC North after Sunday’s win over the Baltimore Ravens. The Browns are winning despite, as ESPN’s Ben Solak highlights , Watson being: fourth in interception/sack rate per dropback at 11.8%, third worst in explosive pass rate at 9.1%, second worst in completion percentage over expectation. Solak also fairly points out that the offensive line is not doing Watson any favors as he is facing the fourth-highest pressure rate among all quarterbacks (40%), and the rushing attack is the worst in the league by success rate (34.4%). Of course, how much of that pressure is due to Watson holding onto the ball forever is open to debate, but there is no doubt he is an equal contributor when it comes to operating under pressure. Now, just because the starting quarterback decision is off head coach Todd Monken’s plate, these are still the Browns, so another in-season decision is looming on the horizon. That is because the club is only one week away from having to determine the makeup of the quarterback room for the rest of the season. Cleveland opened the 21-day practice window for Dillon Gabriel on October 6 , meaning that window comes to a full close on October 27. By then, general manager Andrew Berry and Monken must decide if they are going to: Put Gabriel on the 53-man roster, Return Gabriel to injured reserve for the rest of the season. Trade Gabriel Release Gabriel The decision is complicated by the fact that Shedeur Sanders and rookie Taylen Green are also on the roster, so the Browns must decide if it is smart to keep four quarterbacks on the roster, especially with injuries hitting some other key areas. When Gabriel first came off injured reserve, Monken was asked about the prospect of having four quarterbacks, and he smartly answered that he didn’t have to think about it for three weeks. The Browns can always release Green and sign him back to the practice squad if no one claims him. But that runs the risk of losing the weekly call from some media members for the team to use valuable practice time to develop a “Taylen Green package” to shock and awe opposing defenses. As stated, they could see if another team is interested in Gabriel, who is often described as someone destined to have a career as a reliable backup. So, he has that going for him. Then there is what to do with Sanders, who recently hired an agent in a “nothing to see here, just everyday stuff” move last week? It continues to appear that Sanders will not see the field this season, and the Browns are going to have a new quarterback room in 2027, so could his agent work to see if a deal is out there? Especially as it seems like each week a new team crops up in need of a quarterback? Speaking of which, the Philadelphia Eagles find themselves in a lost season after putting quarterback Jalen Hurts on injured reserve for the rest of the year. And Berry’s twin brother, Adam, just so happens to be the assistant general manager in Philadelphia, so that would be an easy phone call between the two that could result in a deal. But only if both parties are interested, of course. It’s all speculation for now, and the Browns have been busy winning close games to put any public-facing focus on the situation. But the clock is ticking, and by this time next week a decision will have to be made. Whichever way the Browns go, it should make for an interesting day. full_text: This past week, the Cleveland Browns defeated the Baltimore Ravens 13-10 on a beautiful day along the shores of Lake Erie. Prior to the game, I made a trip down to the Muni Lot to soak in the tailgating atmosphere. Many of you know that I love documenting areas around Northeast Ohio as part of my Poko Traveler channel on YouTube, and I’ve had it on my radar for the past few years to capture Browns tailgating in Downtown Cleveland. I wanted to do it when the weather was decent and the team was still competitive, so this was a perfect opportunity to do so. I started down by the Muni Lot, walking up-and-down the paths to give you a taste of what it’s like. And if you’re a regular down there, I’d love for you to chime in on your memories of the area, tailgating traditions, or if you maybe even saw yourself in the video. I continued the video after the Muni Lot, walking over to Huntington Bank Field, and then back toward Downtown Cleveland to see the stream of fans still filing in before kickoff.

title: Browns defense gets huge game from Schwesinger, and these safeties stepped up big
summary: Somehow, the Browns need to fix the fact that they keep allowing opening-drive touchdowns. Imagine if they played shutdown defense right out of the gate, and how that could impact the early flow of the game. Just like they always had Peyton Manning’s number (relatively speaking), they seem to always lock in on Derrick Henry […]
full_text: CLEVELAND, OHIO - OCTOBER 18: Carson Schwesinger #49 of the Cleveland Browns celebrates after a game against the Baltimore Ravens at Huntington Bank Field on October 18, 2026 in Cleveland, Ohio. (Photo by Lauren Leigh Bacho/Getty Images) | Getty Images Somehow, the Browns need to fix the fact that they keep allowing opening-drive touchdowns. Imagine if they played shutdown defense right out of the gate, and how that could impact the early flow of the game. Just like they always had Peyton Manning’s number (relatively speaking), they seem to always lock in on Derrick Henry for whatever reason, compared to other teams. They shut down the Ravens for the final three quarters, a shutout that was necessary to pull off the 13-10 victory. Below, we analyze the snap counts and stats on offense for the Cleveland Browns ’ Week 6 game against the Baltimore Ravens. Defensive Line Pos Player Plays % Snaps Stats DL Maliek Collins 40 70% 1 tackle, 2 assists (3 combined). 1 sack. 1 TFL, 1 QH. DL Jared Verse 38 67% 2 tackles, 1 assist (3 combined). 1 TFL, 1 QH. DL Isaiah McGuire 38 67% 2 tackles, 1 assist (3 combined). 1 sack, 1 TFL, 1 QH. DL Sam Kamara 33 58% 4 tackles (4 combined). 2 TFL. DL Adin Huntington 30 53% 1 tackle (1 combined). 3 QH. DL Sam Williams 21 37% No stats registered. DL Derek Barnett 21 37% 2 assists (2 combined). DL Chris Williams 9 16% 1 assist (1 combined). 1 QH. Maliek Collins is back to the semi-dominant form he displayed a year ago. He logged another sack and was the Browns’ fourth-highest graded defender on PFF, grading out to a 75.0. Imagine this version of Collins paired with when Mason Graham comes back. Adin Huntington and Sam Kamara are starting to stack some respectable performances as depth too, as they combined for tackles for losses and quarterback hits too. I get that Jared Verse is supposedly drawing attention to help others out, as part of the team-first mentality, Still, though, I expect a few high-impact plays from him each week, and they’re still absent from now. The past couple of games, he’s also had late hits on the quarterback that I’ve been stunned weren’t flagged for penalties. Linebacker Pos Player Plays % Snaps Stats LB Carson Schwesinger 57 100% 5 tackles, 8 assists (13 combined). 1 forced fumble. LB Quincy Williams 57 100% 4 tackles, 2 assists (6 combined). 1 sack, 2 QH. I was waiting for that breakout performance from Carson Schwesinger this season, and this was it. And not just because of the fumble he forced on Derrick Henry , although that is certainly a bonus. He led the team with 13 tackles and was a big reason the team’s run defense got it together. He was the team’s second-highest graded defender on the day by PFF, grading out to a 78.2, but his run defense graded out to a 93.1. Quincy Williams , on the other hand, came off his best game with a much more subdued performance, although he still got a sack and another hit on Tyler Huntley . He was the team’s lowest-graded defended by PFF, grading out to a 51.1. Cornerback Pos Player Plays % Snaps Stats CB Denzel Ward 57 100% 1 assist (1 combined). 2 passes defended. CB Tyson Campbell 56 98% 1 assist (1 combined). 1 pass defended, 1 fumble recovery. CB Myles Harden 33 58% 2 tackles, 1 assist (3 combined). 2 passes defended. Denzel Ward and Tyson Campbell were up to the task of stopping the Ravens’ receivers, and it was one of the reasons why Huntley was hit and sacked a number of times, due to coverage sacks. Ward and Campbell both graded above 74.2 by PFF, and Myles Harden has a respectable day too. We saw Cleveland defenders drop a couple of possible interceptions too. Safety Pos Player Plays % Snaps Stats S Grant Delpit 6 11% 2 tackles (2 combined). S Ronnie Hickman 57 100% 4 tackles, 1 assist (5 combined). S Emmanuel McNeil-Warren 54 95% 4 tackles, 2 assists (6 combined). 1 TFL, 1 pass defended. S Daniel Thomas 20 35% 2 tackles, 1 assist (3 combined). 1 TFL. Grant Delpit exited early with an injury, only playing six snaps. That essentially gave the whole game to Emmanuel McNeil-Warren , and everyone will remember the big tackle for loss at the goal line he had when he cut down Henry (even though the Ravens still scored a play later). McNeil-Warren also missed an interception. Reserve Daniel Thomas got some action and was actually the team’s highest-graded defender by PFF at 85.2. Kudos to both guys for stepping up when Delpit went down.

full_text: The list of former Cleveland Browns in the NFL, as well as in other leagues , is quite expansive. Until recently, there were not always success stories on those lists, but Browns fans are passionate about anything and everything connected to their team, including former players (which is why we created our in-5 trivia daily game ). Cleveland’s matchup with the Tennessee Titans was supposed to bring about another blast from the past name: DT Jordan Elliott . The former Texas and Missouri prospect was selected by the Browns in the third round of the 2020 NFL draft, the first under current GM Andrew Berry. After four years in Cleveland, including 35 starts, Elliott signed with the San Francisco 49ers in free agency. After completing his two-year, $9 million contract, Elliott signed a two-year, $8 million deal with the Titans this offseason. After an “incident” at the facility, the Titans chose to release the veteran defensive tackle on Tuesday: The Titans announce they have released DL Jordan Elliott following an Oct. 15 “incident at the team facility.” — Jonathan Jones (@jjones9) October 20, 2026 The full statement from Tennessee on Elliott’s release: #Titans are releasing DT Jordan Elliott. Statement from the team: On Thursday, October 15, there was an incident at our team facility involving Jordan Elliott. Following our review of the incident, we have made the decision to release Elliott from our roster. We will have no… — TURRON DAVENPORT (@TDavenport_NFL) October 20, 2026 Elliott followed Robert Saleh, his defensive coordinator with the Niners, when he signed with the Titans, so the team’s head coach knew the player well. For the Browns, their Week 7 opponent just lost a defensive lineman who has played in 114 snaps so far this season. While Jeffrey Simmons is the big name on the Tennessee defense, Elliott was an important rotational player. Solomon Thomas, Nazir Stackhouse, Timmy Horney, and Jackie Marshall fill out the rest of the Titans defensive tackle depth chart.

title: Browns offense still needs a spark, but these two players stepped up against Ravens
summary: There’s something about the Browns’ offense in the second half that gets clicking. 237 yards of offense on the day doesn’t sound too impressive, but take into consideration that they only had 46 yards of offense in the first half. Ultimately, they actually out-gained the Ravens, thanks to a strong defensive performance. The team playing […]
full_text: CLEVELAND, OHIO - OCTOBER 18: Jaleel McLaughlin #38 of the Cleveland Browns runs the ball against the Baltimore Ravens during the fourth quarter of the game at Huntington Bank Field on October 18, 2026 in Cleveland, Ohio. (Photo by Gregory Shamus/Getty Images) | Getty Images There’s something about the Browns’ offense in the second half that gets clicking. 237 yards of offense on the day doesn’t sound too impressive, but take into consideration that they only had 46 yards of offense in the first half. Ultimately, they actually out-gained the Ravens, thanks to a strong defensive performance. The team playing complete football (i.e. sticking with things to the end) has worked for four close victories, but to take the next step, they have to obviously break out of that trend to the upside. Below, we analyze the snap counts and stats on offense for the Cleveland Browns ’ Week 6 game against the Baltimore Ravens. Quarterback Pos Player Plays % Snaps Stats QB Deshaun Watson 63 100% 16-of-26 (61.5%) for 164 yards. 8 carries, 29 yards (3.6 YPC). It’s tough to say whether things are processing slower for Deshaun Watson , or if players simply weren’t getting open and he doesn’t want to force the turnover because of that. The announcers kept calling out that players weren’t open, and the few replays that they showed were indicating that as well. I think it’s a mixture of both. I don’t see panic from Watson, but at times, he takes off with what looks to be a decent opening to get some positive yardage. That has worked against some teams, but against the Ravens, their defensive front seemed quicker to close the gap and prevent him from escaping. So if that’s the case against a certain defense, Watson has to discover that balance of perhaps hanging in an extra tick and delivering the ball somewhere. I feel like part of the problem was the gameplan to try pushing the ball downfield too much early. Watson has been at his most efficient when he mixes in short read passes through his progressions with the intermediate throws, which we saw him get back to in the second half. PFF graded Watson out to a 56.4 on the day. Running Back Pos Player Plays % Snaps Stats RB Jaleel McLaughlin 39 62% 9 carries, 41 yards (4.6 YPC). 4 catches, 14 yards (4 targets). RB Audric Estime 19 30% 9 carries, 19 yards (2.1 YPC), 1 TD. FB Michael Burton 10 16% 1 carry, 2 yards (2.0 YPC). 0 catches (1 target). It was a solid running day for Jaleel McLaughlin , who offers that ability to shift his way through a small gap. Again, it wasn’t anything crazy, but it was something that made me feel like we have a chance on squeezing some extra yards out via the ground. I feel like Quinshon Judkins would’ve been stuck in that 3.0 YPC territory on those same plays, based on how he’s played this year. McLaughlin was the Browns’ second-highest graded player on offense, grading out to a 76.6. Audric Estime , just signed, got the team’s lone touchdown of the day down at the goal line. Fullback Michael Burton got his first touch of the season, moving the chains on a fourth down play off of a fullback handoff. Wide Receiver Pos Player Plays % Snaps Stats WR Denzel Boston 58 92% 1 catch, 15 yards (5 targets). WR KC Concepcion 51 81% 4 catches, 37 yards (6 targets). 2 carries, 2 yards (2.0 YPC). WR Jerry Jeudy 39 62% 4 catches, 69 yards (4 targets). WR Tylan Wallace 10 16% 1 catch, 12 yards (1 target). WR Isaiah Bond 9 14% No stats registered. WR Malachi Corley 7 11% No stats registered. Welcome back, Jerry Jeudy , He secured the passes thrown to him well, and they all seemed to come at big moments. His snap count usage ticked up a hair from two weeks ago, and he was the Browns’ top-graded receiver this week by PFF, with a grade of 76.1. KC Concepcion also had a big catch late off of a short laser. I liked trying to incorporate him on a jet sweep, but the defensive back played it well. Cleveland was also going to try a trick play with him throwing the ball, but he wisely aborted the play when it was covered. It was the first game where Denzel Boston was a relative non-factor, although Watson did try to loft a touchdown pass to him in the fourth quarter (but it was out of bounds). Tight End Pos Player Plays % Snaps Stats TE Harold Fannin 56 89% 1 catch, 9 yards (3 targets). TE Blake Whiteheart 17 27% 1 catch, 8 yards (1 target). Not much action for the tight ends again this week. After a relatively hot start for Harold Fannin , it seems unusual to not have him targeted or involved much the past two weeks offensively, despite all the snaps he plays. He ended up being the lowest-graded player on offense by PFF, grading out to a 51.6. Offensive Line Pos Player Plays % Snaps Stats OL Spencer Fano 63 100% OL Elgton Jenkins 63 100% OL Austin Barber 63 100% OL Zion Johnson 63 100% OL Tytus Howard 63 100% The offensive line was healthy and played the whole game. Cleveland allowed 5 sacks on the day, but PFF only charged one of those to the offensive line (being on C Elgton Jenkins ). The Browns’ top-graded player on offense this week? Left guard Zion Johnson , although it was mostly for his run-blocking grade, as his pass blocking grade was below everybody else. Tytus Howard and Austin Barber also received solid grades for their job against the Ravens.

summary: As much as the NFL dominates the sports calendar, it is the shortest season of the three historically major sports in the United States. full_text: As much as the NFL dominates the sports calendar, it is the shortest season of the three historically major sports in the United States. It seems like just yesterday the Cleveland Browns were setting their initial 53-man roster and getting ready for Week 1 of the 2026 NFL season . The Browns are now six games into their season, have crossed the quarter pole of the year a couple of weeks ago, and have two other schedule markers just ahead: The NFL trade deadline and their bye week. Could GM Andrew Berry be big game hunting at the deadline, with the potential of a very high pick coming from the Los Angeles Rams due to injury ? Will the roster be resting up for a late playoff push? Will fans, and Cleveland natives like Jason Kelce , have the Browns on their minds at Thanksgiving with family? Here is Cleveland’s schedule, including the deadline and bye week, heading into Turkey Day: 10/25: Away versus the Tennessee Titans 11/1: Away versus the Pittsburgh Steelers 11/8: Away versus the New Orleans Saints 11/10: NFL trade deadline at 4 PM Eastern 11/15: At home versus the Houston Texans 11/22: Bye Week 11/26: Thanksgiving Day A lot to happen between the end of Week 6 and Thanksgiving, especially with three straight road games. The positives are facing the one-win Titans, the Steelers the week after they return from the first game in Paris (amid civil unrest happening in France), and a Saints team that has seen QB Tyler Shough come back to earth pretty quickly. Winning two or all of their next three games could give Berry even more confidence to be aggressive at the deadline. The bye week happening later in the season could give the young Browns roster a chance to recover and any new additions more time to get acclimated to the team. If all that happens, Cleveland fans will be stuffing their faces with good food on Thanksgiving while opening their mouths to talk nothing but the Browns. title: Cleveland native Jason Kelce excited for Browns start, ‘we’ve been waiting for this’
summary: The Cleveland Browns are 4-2, and the bandwagon has room for a lot more to jump on or return to the orange and brown of their youth. While the Browns four wins have not been pretty, with all of them (and the loss to the New York Jets) potentially going the other way, learning to […]
full_text: The Cleveland Browns are 4-2 , and the bandwagon has room for a lot more to jump on or return to the orange and brown of their youth. While the Browns four wins have not been pretty, with all of them (and the loss to the New York Jets) potentially going the other way, learning to win is an important skill for a very young team to learn. Can Cleveland sustain this ? Are the Browns the biggest frauds in the NFL ? Who cares? At least for now, Cleveland fans have something to be excited about, including Jason Kelce. Growing up Browns fans, Jason’s brother Travis begged the team to draft him when he was coming out of the University of Cincinnati. Travis has also been a regular at many other Cleveland teams’ games and bought a ownership stake in the Cleveland Guardians. Jason has been a little less Cleveland-forward in his presentation, until Monday Night Football when he started using the term “we” and a lot of excitement to describe the Browns start to the season: Cleveland native @JasonKelce had a lot to get off his chest after the Browns' 4-2 start 😭 pic.twitter.com/UNHxQDUcT1 — NFL on ESPN (@ESPNNFL) October 19, 2026 Given the Browns positive start, it is possible that the team could get their scheduled flexed in the near future, but probably not to Kelce’s Monday Night Football just yet. No matter what, a fun thing for Cleveland natives and fans is that the Browns are 4-2 and at the top of the AFC North. It is a big deal to see the elder Kelce join his brother in embracing the “we” that is their Cleveland upbringing. That moniker used to only be used by Jason for the Philadelphia Eagles. full_text: (Photo by Lauren Leigh Bacho/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Cleveland Browns have won four of their last five games to reach first place in the AFC North Division. That was so long ago that rookie left tackle Spencer Fano, the youngest player on the current, was just 9 years old at the time. (At least once the game’s first series is in the books.) There are a lot of numbers that stand out when it comes to the defense, but there is one area in particular that we want to highlight. The Baltimore Ravens had put up 30, 41, and 30 points in the three games that quarterback Tyler Huntley started before Sunday’s game. But against the Browns? title: Cowboys at Packers: Dallas potential touchdown is a turning point
summary: For a few seconds on Sunday night, it looked like the Cowboys had found exactly the play they needed. Dee Winters intercepted Jordan Love, got back to his feet and raced into the end zone. With Dallas trailing 7-0, the defense appeared to have delivered a touchdown that would give the Cowboys a chance to […]
full_text: Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images | Getty Images For a few seconds on Sunday night, it looked like the Cowboys had found exactly the play they needed. Dee Winters intercepted Jordan Love, got back to his feet and raced into the end zone. With Dallas trailing 7-0, the defense appeared to have delivered a touchdown that would give the Cowboys a chance to tie the game. Instead, replay ruled Winters down by contact, taking the score away and putting the offense on the field at Green Bay’s 42-yard line. Dallas still had an excellent opportunity. What happened next became the turning point in a 23-13 defeat. The interception itself stood. Matthew Golden’s contact with Winters simply meant the return did not count. That matters here, because the Cowboys still controlled what happened next. They had possession in Packers territory, a manageable deficit and a chance to make their defensive takeaway count. Initially, the offense responded. CeeDee Lamb made a tough 16-yard catch on third-and-three to move Dallas into the red zone. Even after losing the defensive touchdown, the Cowboys were in position to finish the possession with points and put pressure back on Green Bay. Then the opportunity disappeared. Green Bay linebacker Zaire Franklin came through on a delayed blitz and delivered a heavy hit on Dak Prescott. On the following play, facing third-and-eight, Prescott looked for Lamb over the middle. Safety Evan Williams stepped into the throwing lane and intercepted the pass. A possession that began with the celebration of a potential touchdown ended without even a field-goal attempt. That was the damaging part of this sequence. Dallas had already done the difficult work of taking the ball away and moving into scoring position. The Cowboys did not need to force a breakthrough. They needed to protect the opportunity they had created. Instead, Green Bay took possession and kept the Dallas defense on the field for another extended stretch. The Packers put together a 15-play, 73-yard drive that consumed more than eight minutes and ended with a field goal for a 10-0 lead. Dallas had gone from a potential tying score to a two-possession deficit without adding a point. The next Cowboys possession made that missed chance even more costly. A Ryan Flournoy holding penalty wiped out a productive Tyler Goodson run, and Prescott threw another interception after Lamb slipped on his route. Green Bay followed with a touchdown drive to take a 17-0 lead into halftime. Dallas had reached threatening positions on consecutive possessions and come away empty both times. The overturned Winters touchdown will understandably draw attention. But Dallas still had the ball, favorable field position and time to answer. The interception that followed was where that promising moment turned against the Cowboys. On a night when points were difficult to find, Dallas could not afford to waste the opening its defense provided, and that moment became the games turning point.
author: Mike Poland

title: Cowboys rookie report: Packers game exposed some deficiencies
summary: Dallas fell to 2–4 with Sunday’s 23–13 loss at Green Bay. Four rookies played on defense and coverage remained a problem, while the rookie defensive linemen struggled to disrupt Jordan Love. Here is how each rookie fared this week, listed in draft order, and any undrafted players worth noting after that.  Caleb Downs (75 defensive […]
full_text: Photo by Michael Reaves/Getty Images | Getty Images Dallas fell to 2–4 with Sunday’s 23–13 loss at Green Bay. Four rookies played on defense and coverage remained a problem, while the rookie defensive linemen struggled to disrupt Jordan Love. Here is how each rookie fared this week, listed in draft order, and any undrafted players worth noting after that. Caleb Downs (75 defensive snaps | 12 tackles | 0 TFL | 0 sacks | 0 interceptions | 0 passes defended | 1 pressure) Downs stayed busy, finishing with six solo tackles and six assists. However, that production came alongside a difficult coverage night where he allowed six pass completions on six targets for 48 yards. Bringing down those receivers after the catch accounted for most of his tackling stats. He contributed a pressure, but Dallas needs more plays that prevent completions from its first-round safety. Overall, it was a learning night for Downs on the need for tighter coverage in zone and man. Malachi Lawrence (39 defensive snaps | 0 tackles | 0 TFL | 0 sacks | 0 interceptions | 1 pass defended | 0 pressures | 0 QB hits) The pass defended was Lawrence’s only positive contribution on an otherwise quiet night. He registered no pressures across 21 pass-rush snaps. With Dallas needing someone to hurry Love, that was a disappointing return from a substantial opportunity after a week of coaches saying he deserved more snaps and more opportunities. The result was less inspiring this week than his previous week. Jaishawn Barham (60 defensive snaps | 4 tackles | 0 TFL | 0 sacks | 0 interceptions | 0 passes defended | 1 pressure | 1 QB hit) Barham’s performance split sharply between run defense and coverage. He made three very good run stops and had no missed tackles against the run, but he missed a key tackle against the pass on third down that extended a touchdown drive for the Packers. He also allowed five catches on six targets for 82 yards. His work near the line was the most encouraging and was excellent at meeting the run or getting the Green Bay’s backfield. But containing receivers remains an area to much improve. LT Overton (22 defensive snaps | 0 tackles | 0 TFL | 0 sacks | 0 interceptions | 0 passes defended | 0 pressures | 0 QB hits) Overton played after entering the weekend questionable with a foot injury. He generated no pressures on 16 pass-rush snaps and did not register a single tackle. Availability was the most positive takeaway here, but his individual production was limited and the defense really did need more.

title: 2026 NFL Week 7 Power Rankings: Cowboys continue to plummet
summary: The Dallas Cowboys refuse to rise to the occasion. Last week it was taking care of business at home against a team they were huge favorites against. While it was more to expect them to travel and emerge victorious as underdogs, the expectation was to at the very least compete. They did not. A month […]
full_text: Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images | Getty Images The Dallas Cowboys refuse to rise to the occasion. Last week it was taking care of business at home against a team they were huge favorites against. While it was more to expect them to travel and emerge victorious as underdogs, the expectation was to at the very least compete. They did not. A month and change ago the national narrative around this team was that they had a very quiet offseason and had built a team that could legitimately challenge to finally end The Drought™. They are fortunate to play in an NFC East this season where they still might win it despite their 2-4 record, but right now they don’t look like they can put an end to anything let alone the shadow that has lived over the franchise for a generation. It will come as no surprise to see that the Cowboys have really fallen in our power rankings and in those from across the internet. On with the show. 1 – San Francisco 49ers (LW: 1) It must be nice to be home favorites against a bad team and show up in a way where you dominate them. 2 – Buffalo Bills (LW: 2) If you are a Bills fan you have to be slightly worried that they are peaking too soon, right? Or do only we have those insecurities? 3 – Kansas City Chiefs (LW: 3) They are back and better than ever. Not really, but Kenneth Walker is such a cheat code for them. 4 – New England Patriots (LW: 6) Reports of their demise were seemingly incorrect! 5 – Detroit Lions (LW: 8) Back from the bye. 6 – Jacksonville Jaguars (LW: 5) It was certainly not idea to lose to the Texans and give them life. They will be alright, though. Travis Hunter is really finding his NFL form. 7 – Baltimore Ravens (LW: 4) They need Lamar Jackson back in the worst way. 8 – Green Bay Packers (LW: 16) Deep sigh. Th edeepest of sighs. 9 – Chicago Bears (LW: 11) They almost blew it against Atlanta, but a win is a win and this one came with Caleb Williams so things likely feel more normal than they have in some time. 10 – Carolina Panthers (LW: 15) It feels like we are still sleeping on this team. They are so much fun and have serious offensive firepower. I know that Philly was down, but the Panthers are legit. 11 – Seattle Seahawks (LW: 7) They have a quarterback issue, but when you win a Super Bowl (not that we would know what that’s like lately) you are likely less upset when things aren’t going perfectly immediately after. 12 – Minnesota Vikings (LW: 9) Also back from some rest. 13 – Cincinnati Bengals (LW: 10) Them, too! 14 – Houston Texans (LW: 22) It is amazing how good 2-4 must feel to them compared to how it feels to us. 15 – Denver Broncos (LW: 12) Obviously they won, but wow they have serious quarterback problems. It is hard to trust them long-term. 16 – Cleveland Browns (LW: 24) Who would have thought? What a weird surprise! 17 – Pittsburgh Steelers (LW: 17) Mike McCarthy is finding a way. Good for him. 18 – Los Angeles Rams (LW: 13) They are very, very far from being the super power they were hyped up to be. 19 – Las Vegas Raiders (LW: 21) This team is a ton of fun. Maybe they can sneak in as the third Wild Card when it is all said and done. Whatever the case, Klint Kubiak was very clearly the right hire. 20 – Atlanta Falcons (LW: 14) Can you believe that they are legitimately getting production out of Kyle Pitts? Finally! 21 – Arizona Cardinals (LW: 29) They are definitely going to blow out the Cowboys in a couple of weeks. Right? 22 – New Orleans Saints (LW: 26) Kellen Moore stopped the skid! 23 – New York Giants (LW: 18) The NFC East is terrible, but they might be the least terrible. 24 – Dallas Cowboys (LW: 19) They definitely are not. 25 – Philadelphia Eagles (LW: 20) All the best to Jalen Hurts. 26 – Indianapolis Colts (LW: 23) Chris Ballard is finally gone. A selling of assets feels imminent, and likely a head coach change. 27 – Tampa Bay Buccaneers (LW: 25) So Jalon Daniels isn’t the greatest quarterback of all time? 28 – New York Jets (LW: 27) It was a tough scene that Aaron Glenn did not know that the Jets did not get the ball to start the second half. 29 – Washington Commanders (LW: 28) It was also tough that Dan Quinn did not know when it was a fourth down. 30 – Tennessee Titans (LW: 32) They won a game! 31 – Los Angeles Chargers (LW: 30) They still have not. 32 – Miami Dolphins (LW: 31) Yikes. ESPN : 20 (LW: 15) Here we go. Biggest issue on offense: Lack of consistency in the running game The Cowboys’ running game is off to its worst start — 456 yards in six games — since 1989, the year before Emmitt Smith showed up. Six different running backs have more total rushing yards than the Cowboys. Javonte Williams has seven rushing touchdowns, but the inconsistency and lack of attempts are killing the offense. Coordinator Klayton Adams said last week the Cowboys are being forced to play with one arm tied behind their back because they can’t run it well enough. That has impacted the passing game, too. Quarterback Dak Prescott was under duress on 21 of his 41 second-half pass attempts against Green Bay, averaging only 4.8 yards per attempt. — Todd Archer NFL.com : 26 (LW: 18) The first line is fair. I’ve lost all faith in the Cowboys. The offense was their lone strength, but it has devolved into a mess of an operation. Their quarterback isn’t adjusting to a consistently messy post-snap picture, and Dallas’ chances of victory have evaporated. We already knew this defense was a problem, but the offense’s regression has escalated this situation from general concern to something bordering on catastrophe. It’s a shame, too, because the NFC East has never been more winnable. As of now, I don’t think it’ll be the Cowboys finishing on top. USA Today : 26 (LW: 24) Another drop. “GOTI,” aka, Greatest Offense There Is? It’s nice to have goals. Not always wise to publicly reveal them. Yahoo : 21 (LW: 20) Only a slight dip here. Nobody questioned the Cowboys’ offense. Through four games Dallas averaged 30.5 points per game and was third in the NFL in EPA per play, trailing only San Francisco and Buffalo. Then, over the last two games, its offense has disappeared against Tampa Bay and Green Bay, neither of which has a great defense. The Cowboys are averaging 14.5 points over their last two games and slipped to 19th in EPA per play. Their defense isn’t good enough to overcome that. “Because of the lack of a running game, we’re a little bit one-sided and the best way to be on offense as a unit is to have balance,” Cowboys head coach Brian Schottenheimer said, according to ESPN. The running game is a problem. Dallas has just 98 rushing yards total over the last two games, it has reached 100 yards in a game just once and rank 31st in rushing yards per game. It’s also accurate that the Cowboys looked completely unprepared for a blitz-heavy approach from the Packers, and that could be a coaching issue. Perhaps getting the run game going will dissuade future opponents from blitzing on most downs. CBS Sports : 19 (LW: 17) Still inside the top 20. The offense is suddenly having some issues, which I didn’t see coming. But in their bad division, there is still time to turn it around, starting this week at Philadelphia. The Athletic : 22 (LW: 20) Right behind the Eagles and Giants. The only people associated with the Cowboys who are happy at the moment are Lamb’s fantasy managers. He’s ninth in scoring (21.9 ppg) and third in the league in receiving yards (577). He was targeted 18 times Sunday night and finished with nine catches for 70 yards. ProFootballTalk : 23 (LW: 20) And there it is. Cheap does as cheap is. Week To Week Movement Full Power Rankings

title: Brian Schottenheimer report card: A second straight dud from the head coach
summary: I would like to start the week six Brian Schottenheimer report card with his grade against the Green Bay Packers. F. Thank you for reading. Okay, okay, okay, let’s actually dive into this. You could make the argument that the week six trip to Green Bay was the biggest game for the Cowboys so far […]
full_text: Photo by David Buono/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images I would like to start the week six Brian Schottenheimer report card with his grade against the Green Bay Packers. F. Thank you for reading. Okay, okay, okay, let’s actually dive into this. You could make the argument that the week six trip to Green Bay was the biggest game for the Cowboys so far this season. After embarrassing themselves on both sides of the football against the then 0-4 Tampa Bay Buccaneers, the Cowboys had a really good opportunity to get back to .500 on the season with a quality road win, against a quality road opponent. The result? Maybe the team’s most embarrassing performance we have seen in quite some time (well, except for last week). The frustration with Schottenheimer started before the ball was even kicked. One of the easiest things a head coach can do for their football team is give yourself a chance to double up on points by deferring after winning the coin toss. Instead, the Cowboys handed the Packers that opportunity on a silver platter. People argue taking the football first can allow you to set the tone, but with how poorly the Cowboys defense has played so far this season, there is no tone to set. Instead, the Cowboys had a six play, 19-yard drive, and punted the ball right to Green Bay, who then went on a 14-play, 90-yard drive to take the lead, and they never looked back. If you thought the Cowboys offense struggled last week against Tampa, boy it was so much worse Sunday night in Green Bay. The Cowboys struggled to run the ball all night, averaging 3.1 yards per carry when you remove Dak Prescott’s scramble yards. They also struggled to gain any consistency through the air, while dropping back to pass 54 times. Those drop backs were a struggle all night and pretty much everyone involves deserves blame but today were grading Brian Schottenheimer. Schottenheimer has been a net-negative to the team in back-to-back weeks. His lack of creativity, answers versus the blitz, and route concepts are just nowhere near good enough to give the offense any easy buttons. After watching the All-22, we can confirm what Chris Collinsworth and Mike Tirico alluded to many times last night. The banged up Green Bay defense were not afraid of the Cowboys passing attack. They sent heavy blitzes all night because the play-calling to beat the blitz was bad, and the pass protection rules Schottenheimer’s offense has put on tape the last few weeks gives the defense an easy advantage. They left their depth cornerbacks on an island often against CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens, because they were not afraid of them beating them vertically. The last two weeks, Schottenheimer’s offense has been neutered, and so far, the “answers” they have put on tape are just “hopefully our players can be better”. Well, they haven’t been. While the play-calling has been bad, and the answers versus the blitz have been bad, the game management and game preparation has been even worse on the offensive side of the ball. Going back to the decision to take the ball to start the game, Brian Schottenheimer elected to punt on 4th and 4 from the Green Bay 47. The third-down call that put them in fourth in manageable was a designed swing pass to Javonte Williams in the flat. An aggressive, tone-setting team likely runs the football on third down and knows before the third-down play is snapped that we are setting the tone by going for it on fourth down. Schottenheimer then called a timeout on defense in the second quarter on fourth-down for no reason, as Matt LaFluer came out on fourth-down from the two, tried the hard count, and took a delay of game and kicked the 25-yard field goal. Schottenheimer then used his second and third timeout with :28 seconds left in the first half, with the Packers offense scoring on a Jordan Love rushing touchdown with :23 seconds left in the first half. The game preparation stuff showed up next, as the Cowboys offense looked to get into field goal range before halftime with 23 seconds left. Dak Prescott completed a six-yard pass to Jake Ferguson in bounds but forgot to carry the football back to the line of scrimmage and the Cowboys were unable to get another play off before the clock hit 0:00. In reality, this did not impact the game, but these are small details the Schottenheimer-led offense cannot be making in year two under his supervision. We could go on and on about all the issues, but the reality is none of it is good right now. Since beating the Texans in week four, the Cowboys have played just as poorly on offense as they have on defense. Opposing defensive coordinators now realize the play designs and protection rules the Cowboys are putting on tape are making things pretty much impossible on the Cowboys passing game, and until that changes, they will continue to struggle to move the football with any consistency through the air or ground. If you would like to see every third-down attempt up until the mid-way point of the fourth quarter (when the game was pretty much over), you can see them here: Thread of every third down from the Cowboys loss last night. Tell me what you see — Connor Livesay (@ConnorNFLDraft) October 19, 2026 Play-Calling F Fourth-Down Decisions F The decision to punt on the first drive was a pretty big whiff from Schotty. Late in the third quarter, he also decided to punt down 20-7 with 3:35 remaining on 4th and 7 from about midfield. Sure, if they fail to get that the game is probably over, but better third-down play calling could make these fourth-down decisions much easier, especially late in games. Timeout Usage F Team Preparation F It was all pretty ugly, again. What grade would you give to Brian Schottenheimer on Sunday?

title: Brian Schottenheimer’s timeout decisions were suspect at best
summary: If you simulated Sunday night’s Dallas Cowboys game against the Green Bay Packers 100 times then the visitors probably lose a significant majority of them. I don’t know how you could argue otherwise right now. In reality the Cowboys did lose, 23-23, and did so in a way that the final score doesn’t properly reflect. […]
full_text: Mandatory Credit: Jeff Hanisch-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect If you simulated Sunday night’s Dallas Cowboys game against the Green Bay Packers 100 times then the visitors probably lose a significant majority of them. I don’t know how you could argue otherwise right now. In reality the Cowboys did lose, 23-23, and did so in a way that the final score doesn’t properly reflect. There were a lot of things wrong with what Dallas did at Lambeau Field, but one thing was really difficult to process as it was unfolding in real time: Brian Schottenheimer’s timeout strategy. Schottenheimer’s timeout decisions were suspect at best Let’s set the stage. After the Dak Prescott interception where CeeDee Lamb fell down the Packers took over at their own 23-yard line with 1:50 left before halftime. They had all 3 of their timeouts, and the Cowboys had 2 remaining. It should also be noted that the Packers were set to receive the second half kickoff given that Dallas took the ball when they won the opening coin toss. The Packers began to move, and following a Joey Porter Jr. pass interference they had a new set of downs at the Dallas 27-yard line. At this point there was 53 seconds left and Green Bay had burnt one of their timeouts. Green Bay handed the ball off to Pierre Strong and he picked up 4 yards. The clock showed 46 seconds left and a timeout was called. NBC’s Mike Tirico was setting up a point about how the Packers were burning one of theirs, and then seemed surprised that the Cowboys were the team who called it. “And the Packers… hold on to those two timeouts. Now one is taken… by Dallas, I believe.” When the broadcast came back from commercial Tirico speculated that maybe the Cowboys wanted to save hope of getting the ball back before halftime. Sure, that is plausible in a literal sense. But a few plays later the Packers converted another third down (shocker) by way of Jordan Love finding Matthew Golden. Golden came down in bound sat the Dallas 2-yard line. Brian Schottenheimer called his final timeout. Why? What could the strategy have possibly been at this point? Tirico was similarly sort of shocked as he was setting the stage. “Clock continues to run. 28 seconds, it’s first and goal. And a timeout taken… Dallas takes its final timeout before first and goal.” The absolute best explanation you can come up with here is that Schottenheimer was trying to get his defense set. Maybe the most obvious answer is the actual one. But each of these times the timeouts were called right away. If Schottenheimer wanted to change personnel he could have let the Packers line up and then called it. At least that way more time would have been burned off of the clock. He literally called each of these two timeouts at the time that most benefitted Green Bay. Look at in the game log. It is difficult to understand. The only real explanation is that Schottenheimer maybe somehow believed that Dallas was going to have time to mount a drive themselves? But even then, that is a huge stretch. The situations in question would have involved time running out before at the very least a Packers field goal and that would have left the Cowboys with very little time (and no timeouts!) to give a possession their full go. Again, I’d be willing to buy the theory that he wanted to get the defense set if he at least let some time trickle off the clock. But he did not. This is very difficult to explain.

title: Cowboys at Packers: Joey Porter Jr. makes his presence felt in tough loss
summary: Week 6 was seen as a turning point for the 2026 Dallas Cowboys. After an embarrassing home loss to the Tampa Bay Buccaneers 10 days earlier, Dallas discussed plenty of big-picture questions during its mini bye week. From the coaches and players, we heard this team was ready to turn the page and not let […]
full_text: (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images Week 6 was seen as a turning point for the 2026 Dallas Cowboys. After an embarrassing home loss to the Tampa Bay Buccaneers 10 days earlier, Dallas discussed plenty of big-picture questions during its mini bye week. From the coaches and players, we heard this team was ready to turn the page and not let their abysmal performance in Week 5 be a sign of things to come. There was some optimism heading into their matchup against the Green Bay Packers, but after a 23-13 loss in which the score was not indicative of how close the teams were on the field, that optimism seems to be all but gone. Dallas got both outperformed and outcoached in a big way on Sunday night. While their defense did perform a bit better, it still didn’t resemble anything close to even a league-average unit. To the shock of many, Dallas’ offense was even worse than the defense. Dak Prescott and company looked out of sync all night long as the Packers’ defense dominated the matchup. There weren’t many positives to take away from this game, but one lone bright spot was cornerback Joey Porter Jr. In his second game as a Cowboy, the former Steeler performed very well, earning him this week’s game ball award. In 28 coverage snaps, Porter did not allow a single reception, while posting an excellent 39.6 Passer Rating against. Porter also recorded an impressive PBU on a deep ball to Packers wideout Matthew Golden, saving Dallas’ defense from allowing another touchdown. Joey Porter Jr. was with him step-for-step DALvsGB on NBC/Peacock Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/8AgCGjPZPp — NFL (@NFL) October 19, 2026 Joey Porter Jr is having a night! #SFSP pic.twitter.com/xcl0NEqKwc — Oliver Davis II (@I_Am_OD3) October 19, 2026 If there is one positive to come out of the Green Bay matchup, it’s that Joey Porter Jr. looks like a true number one lockdown corner. If he can stay healthy and help slow down teams’ number-one offensive targets week in and week out, it will greatly help Daron Bland, Shavon Revel, and other members of Dallas’ secondary who have been struggling to this point in the season.

title: History says Cowboys will be patient with Brian Schottenheimer
summary: The Dallas Cowboys have only two wins through their first six games for just the 16th time in franchise history. Amazingly, and unfortunately, this has now been the case for them in back-to-back seasons. Brian Schottenheimer’s direct predecessors each oversaw only one start to a season of this variety. For Mike McCarthy (2020), Jason Garrett […]
full_text: Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images | Getty Images The Dallas Cowboys have only two wins through their first six games for just the 16th time in franchise history. Amazingly, and unfortunately, this has now been the case for them in back-to-back seasons. Brian Schottenheimer’s direct predecessors each oversaw only one start to a season of this variety. For Mike McCarthy (2020), Jason Garrett (2015), and Wade Phillips (2010) mid-October saw them lead the Cowboys to at least a hat trick’s worth of wins more often than not. Schottenheimer is the subject of great focus for the Cowboys right now and as a result some on the internet are wondering if the Cowboys could look to make a move. You will of course be shocked to learn that the team’s brass said that is in no way on their minds at the moment. Cowboys EVP Stephen Jones on @1053thefan said they “absolutely” believe in Brian Schottenheimer. “There’s not any question in Jerry and my mind. He has the team. There’s no question they want to go out there and execute and make things happen. Feel really good about our coaching… — Jon Machota (@jonmachota) October 19, 2026 You can file this under “what else are they supposed to say” as the Cowboys know that they are in a bad NFC East and could wind up winning it when this calendar year wraps. Even if that happens, it is hard to see how the critics will cool on Brian Schottenheimer. Winning does cure all, though. If you are curious what would happen if the wheels continued to fall off, it isn’t exactly the Cowboys’ style to fire coaches midseason. Heck, it isn’t even their style (relative to modern times) to fire them at all. Wade Phillips was the last head coach who the Cowboys paid to not work for them, and they infamously fired him after a Sunday Night Football loss to the Green Bay Packers at Lambeau Field. Sound familiar? As many have said over the last decade and a half, the Cowboys were clearly comfortable doing that then because they had what they saw to be as an obvious replacement on staff already in Jason Garrett. Garrett did become the next head coach, and he was never fired by the team. The Cowboys saw his contract through twice. It was after that second one came to an end that Dallas chose to simply not bring him back. They, as you know, brought in Mike McCarthy (who coincidentally delivered the final blow to Wade Phillips that fateful night at Lambeau) and he also saw his contract run through before he and the team went their separate ways. This leads us to our present time. Schottenheimer signed a four-year deal with the Cowboys when they brought him on in 2025. This means that he isn’t even halfway done which is why the historical context is necessary here. History says the Cowboys will hold. What do you think, though? Do you think it’s possible this is the time that they buck that trend? Or do you expect more of the same in that capacity?

title: Denver’s best things to do, see, and eat before heading to a Broncos game
summary: Denver has one of the best home-field advantages in the NFL. It’s also one of the best places to watch a game, even if you’re not a fan of the Denver Broncos. While Empower Field at Mile High Stadium may not have the history of old Mile High Stadium, the vibe remains the same, thanks […]
full_text: DENVER, CO - SEPTEMBER 20: Denver Broncos fan Robert Ramirez swings his Home Opener themed towel during the first quarter of a game against the Jacksonville Jaguars on Sunday, Sept. 20, 2026, at Empower Field at Mile High in Denver, Colo. (Photo by Timothy Hurst/MediaNews Group/The Denver Post via Getty Images) | Denver Post via Getty Images Denver has one of the best home-field advantages in the NFL. It’s also one of the best places to watch a game, even if you’re not a fan of the Denver Broncos. While Empower Field at Mile High Stadium may not have the history of old Mile High Stadium, the vibe remains the same, thanks to Broncos Country … albeit the South Stands are calmer nowadays. Denver is also one of the best cities in the US, and, no, I don’t care if there’s bias in that. It’s the truth. For those coming to the Mile High City for the first time, or even if you’re an experienced traveler, here are some of the best things to do, see, and eat before heading to a Denver Broncos game. If that wasn’t enough, we’ve thrown in how to get to the stadium, and the best things to do when you get there. Places to stay in Denver Let’s preface this section by saying that if you’re coming to the Mile High City for a Broncos game, you’ll want to make your trip as easy as possible. So, for the hotels, let’s aim for downtown Denver or LoDo (AKA Lower Downtown). Rates listed are as of mid-October, mid-week, so they will vary by date. The Oxford Hotel The oldest grand hotel in Denver, if you’re looking for history, the Oxford has it in spades. What makes this hotel a great choice, aside from the history, is the location. The Oxford Hotel is around a 1-minute walk to Union Station. For those going to a Broncos game, it means premium access to Mile High Stadium (see more on that below). But on top of all of that, you’re within walking distance to Larimer Square and the 16th Street Mall, which offer all sorts of restaurants and various activities. What makes the Oxford even better is the Cruise Room . It’s a circa-1920s speakeasy with fantastic classic drinks and a very cool vibe. Definitely worth checking out, even if you don’t stay at the Oxford on your trip. From Google: “Denver’s oldest grand hotel, blending 1890s opulence with the iconic Art Deco Cruise Room martini bar.” Rates start at $214 per night. Hotel Teatro Another classy, refined hotel offering direct access to the Denver theater district and the Colorado Convention Center. So you could swing a play at the Denver City for the Performing Arts , maybe an opera at the classic opera house, before going to the game. The 1911 Hotel Teatro is also right by the Denver Theater Light Rail station to help wth getting to the stadium on gameday. Located in the middle of Downtown Denver, you have walking access to the 16th Street Mall, and with it, restaurants. As it says on Google, “Sophisticated historic landmark situated directly across from the theater district offering zero-fee pet policies and cozy elegance.“ Rates start at $129 per night. Populus Denver This is one of the most distinctive-looking hotels in Denver, featuring biophilic design. The Populus Denver is also an eco-conscious boutique hotel just a 2-minute walk from Civic Center Park and the state capitol building. You’re also close to the Denver Art Museum. Further east in downtown Denver than the choices listed above, you still have access to the 16th Street Mall and the restaurants in the area. Unlike the other two, you’ll likely have to take an RTD bus west down the 16th Street Mall to get to the Light Rail Station for access to the stadium. Another option is a rideshare from this hotel. From Google: “Sustainable dining, and corner suites overlooking Civic Center Park and the Capitol.” Rates start at $178 per night. Things to do in Denver There is so much to do in and around Denver that you could spend a week in the Mile High City and not scratch the surface. The list already started with some things to do around the hotel recommendations, so here are some more popular and unique things to check out in Denver. Red Rocks You can’t visit Denver without checking the concert list to see who is performing at Red Rocks . Obviously, this depends on the time of year, but everyone should have attending a concert at Red Rocks on their bucket list. Heck, even if there isn’t a concert at Red Rocks, you can still check out the venue during the day. You’ll have to use a rideshare option, unless you rent a car for your trip. There are no Light Rail stops at Red Rocks. Molly Brown House Museum Made famous for surviving the sinking of the Titanic, the woman, popularly known as the Unsinkable Molly Brown and Heroine of the Titanic, rendered amazing service to survivors. Visiting the museum is worth the trip back in time for adults and kids. Based on the recommendations for where to stay, you’ll likely need to take a rideshare to the museum. You could get there on foot, but it would be a jaunt. Buying tickets in advance is recommended; tickets start at $26. Downtown Aquarium This option is more for families with kids. If you’re looking for a world-class aquarium, like the Georgia Aquarium in Atlanta, the Downtown Aquarium won’t come close to that. But it’s worth exploring and spending a few hours seeing the aquatic life in downtown Denver. It’s quaint and worth the trip, as long as you keep an open mind. Meow Wolf Denver If you’ve never experienced Meow Wolf, it’s a must-see experience. There is really nothing like it. It’s like walking into another planet on acid. We’ll leave it at that. Meow Wolf Denver is located right by Mile High, so it’s a great location. Tickets for the experience start at $38. Butterfly Pavilion This is one of the coolest and most unique places in the Denver metro area. The Butterfly Pavilion is great for families and adults. It opened on July 15, 1995, and was the first stand-alone non-profit insect zoo in the United States.” Since the pavilion is located in Westminster, which is west of Denver, you’ll need to use a rideshare to get there. But it’s worth it for the unforgettable experience. Best places to eat in Denver Denver is home to some fantastic and unique restaurants that cover any and all palates. There are far more than can be included on this list, so feel free to search before your trip. But these restaurants are tried-and-true Colorado. Casa Bonita This just goes without saying, right? It’s like Red Rocks. You can’t have a Colorado list of places to eat without the Colorado restaurant. The pink building, famous for cliff divers and sopapillas, is now owned by Trey Parker and Matt Stone (creators of South Park). It’s back and taking reservations . I have not been there since the two bought Casa Bonita, but they promised to upgrade the food. I’m sure it’s better now, but that’s not why you go to Casa Bonita. It’s for the experience. Add it to your list, and you won’t regret it. You’ll need to get there via a rideshare unless you rent a car. It’s located on West Colfax. The Buckhorn Exchange This is another true Colorado eatery. Widely recognized as Denver’s oldest continuously operating restaurant, it was founded in 1893. Then it was a saloon known as The Rio Grande Exchange. Now, it’s a steakhouse that is way more than your average “steakhouse.” As it says on Google, “Where mounted game gaze on dishes of yak, ostrich, elk & Rocky Mountain oysters.” What’s great about the Buckhorn Exchange is that it’s right by a Light Rail station, so it’s easy access. Cherry Cricket — Downtown If you love burgers, this restaurant is for you. Cherry Cricket has some of the best burgers in Denver, and it’s in a great location if you stay downtown (as we recommended). From Google, “Long-running hub with build-your-own burgers among other American staples & a large beer selection.” My Brother’s Bar As it says on the restaurant’s website , “the oldest bar in Denver, continuously serving fine beers and spirits since 1873.” Now it serves up great…

title: Riley Moss or Ja’Quan McMillian? Which CB should the Broncos re-sign?
summary: The Denver Broncos are 4-2 and enjoyed a mini bye week this weekend after their thrilling overtime victory over the defending Super Bowl Champion Seattle Seahawks on Thursday Night Football. During this period, all the attention has been on quarterback Bo Nix and the struggling Denver Broncos offense, and rightfully so. However, the Broncos have […]
full_text: Oct 27, 2024; Denver, Colorado, USA; Denver Broncos cornerback Ja'Quan McMillian (29) celebrates his turnover with cornerback Riley Moss (21) in the second half against the Carolina Panthers at Empower Field at Mile High. Mandatory Credit: Ron Chenoy-Imagn Images | USA TODAY Sports via Reuters Con The Denver Broncos are 4-2 and enjoyed a mini bye week this weekend after their thrilling overtime victory over the defending Super Bowl Champion Seattle Seahawks on Thursday Night Football. During this period, all the attention has been on quarterback Bo Nix and the struggling Denver Broncos offense, and rightfully so. However, the Broncos have another question they have to be thinking about, and it has to do with their secondary. Both starting corners, Riley Moss and Ja’Quan McMillian, will be free agents at the end of the season and, in all likelihood, the team will have to pick one or the other when it comes to re-signing them. We are currently entering Week 7 of the 2026 NFL season, and neither player has received an extension as of yet. So, the question should be asked. Which corner should the Broncos sign to an extension or re-sign this offseason? I posed this question to our Twitter/X followers and received nearly 2,500 responses, most of which were in favor of re-signing cornerback Ja’Quan McMillian. A whopping 93.4% of the voters chose McMillian over Moss. We're 6 games through the 2026 season, so let's revisit this question. Both Riley Moss and Ja'Quan McMillan will be free agents this offseason, which one do you want the team to re-sign? — MileHighReport (@MileHighReport) October 18, 2026 So now, I ask you, Mile High Report: as of right now, which Broncos cornerback should the Broncos re-sign? Riley Moss or Ja’Quan McMillian? Based on the Broncos’ first 6 games of the season, McMillian seems like the better answer. Moss has been dealing with injuries, while McMillian has been very good once again and continues to make impact plays on the field. He had the game-ending sack vs. the Chargers a few weeks ago and had another clutch INT in overtime vs. the Seahawks, which led to the Broncos kicking the game-winning field goal. Also, we know about McMillian’s heroics in the postseason. He has that clutch gene and has become one of the better slot corners in the NFL. Moss has been solid this season as well. He had an INT vs. the Jaguars, which helped spark their second-half comeback in the game, and has played well opposite Pat Surtain II. Unfortunately, he suffered a rib injury vs. the 49ers, missed the game vs. the Chargers, and was very limited vs. the Seahawks. However, when out there, he gives the Broncos a talented boundary cornerback who can match up against bigger, stronger, and faster wide receivers. When making this decision, the Broncos need to factor in their young depth on the roster. Former first-round pick Jahdae Barron played 100% of the snaps vs. the Seahawks and played well, while reserve Kris Abrams-Draine also played very well and had an interception. If you let one of them walk, you have built-in replacements ready and waiting. As for my opinion on this, I am going with Ja’Quan McMillian. This is not a knock on Riley Moss, who I believe is a very good player. It just comes down to what I believe is more valuable. Talented slot corners are not easy to find, and McMillian is one of the best in the NFL. Barron and Abrams-Draine have proven they can play outside and could step in and replace Moss. Also, it’s the impact plays. J-Mac has several clutch game-ending, game-changing, or game-winning plays throughout his career. I want that type of player in my secondary moving forward. Now, I ask you, Mile High Report. When it comes down to Riley Moss and Ja’Quan McMillian, who do you want the Broncos to re-sign/extend?
author: Scotty Payne

title: Stop blaming Bo
summary: Good morning, Broncos Country! Everyone, just freakin’ relax on the QB play, will you? The second question at yesterday’s presser with Sean Payton was wondering if the head coach had considered replacing Bo Nix. What are you even talking about? I’m a big fan of Jarrett Stidham as our backup. If Nix goes down, he’s […]
full_text: DENVER, COLORADO - OCTOBER 15: Bo Nix #10 of the Denver Broncos walks off the field after winning in overtime against the Seattle Seahawks at Empower Field At Mile High on October 15, 2026 in Denver, Colorado. (Photo by Justin Edmonds/Getty Images) | Getty Images Good morning, Broncos Country! Everyone, just freakin’ relax on the QB play, will you? The second question at yesterday’s presser with Sean Payton was wondering if the head coach had considered replacing Bo Nix. What are you even talking about? I’m a big fan of Jarrett Stidham as our backup. If Nix goes down, he’s a very capable QB who knows Payton’s system (and that’s something!) and has enough experience to not be completely overwhelmed. But come on. Benching your starter when the entire offense (and the offensive coaching staff, mind you) is underperforming, is as close to knee-jerk as you can get. Nix is the starter, and struggling against a top-ranked defense is no reason to put in a backup who will likely fare no better, will probably fare worse, and will kill whatever morale is left with an offense that knows it has to do better and that one player is not the problem. Not the only problem anyway. Bo Nix may not be living up to his potential, but neither is Sean Payton or the entire offense. Don't blame Bo (only). But instead, enjoy this #Broncos ' defense AND 4-2! https://t.co/qZl83EQthQ — Doctor of Words (@docllv) October 18, 2026 Payton had a lot more patience than I would have with the benching question. “To answer your question, no. He’s going to become the byproduct of all the finer things that get improved,” Payton said, noting that better play from the O-line, better run-pass balance and better run game performance overall will go a long way in helping Nix. “That’s our jobs as coaches here. We talked after the game about we’re excited to get that win, and yet at the same time find that improvement we need in all areas. So, it starts with all of us.” Payton also played down that Nix was suffering from any mental hurdles after coming back from injury. “This is a tough league. We hit every aspect, and I think that’s one of the things that attracted us to Bo in the beginning is we had seen his ability to climb through adversity,” Payton added. “It’s not just Bo that feels that. Right now, offensively, I feel that, our players feel that and we’ll improve.” Immediately following the Broncos’ win over the Seahawks — and the ensuing meltdown from Ryan Fitzpatrick that provided great TV drama for a day — Tim Jenkins spoke the real truth. If anything, Broncos Country should be encouraged that this team is winning in spite of its underperforming offense. And he also pointed out several instances where just because the play didn’t develop as planned or designed, it didn’t mean it was due to poor QB play. And in response to Fitzpatrick’s primary criticism that Nix wasn’t “playing competitive football” because he didn’t get a first down one-on-one versus a 250-pound linebacker, Jenkins was all over it. “Would I love to see Nix make the linebacker miss one-on-one and get a first down? Sure. Who wouldn’t? Do I think that’s a fair criticism in the National Football League that a quarterback didn’t make a linebacker miss one-on-one? No,” he said. “That’s potentially the dumbest thing I’ve heard all day. And I have five kids 9 and under, so I hear dumb stuff all day long.” Ease up, Broncos Country. There’s a lot to fix, but they’ll get it done. Reminder what our QB can do… https://t.co/Tf6nt1ycWQ — Doctor of Words (@docllv) October 19, 2026
