title: Detroit Lions scouting report: Green Bay’s wild season is trending up
summary: After a much-needed bye week, the Detroit Lions are back on the field. They kick off their 2026 campaign to reclaim their NFC North crown against the Green Bay Packers in Ford Field in Week 7. After back-to-back road games and a bye week, Lions fans should be going crazy for them on Sunday afternoon. […]
full_text: GREEN BAY, WISCONSIN - OCTOBER 18: Matthew Golden #0 of the Green Bay Packers celebrates a touchdown with fans during the first quarter against the Dallas Cowboys at Lambeau Field on October 18, 2026 in Green Bay, Wisconsin. (Photo by Michael Reaves/Getty Images) | Getty Images After a much-needed bye week, the Detroit Lions are back on the field. They kick off their 2026 campaign to reclaim their NFC North crown against the Green Bay Packers in Ford Field in Week 7. After back-to-back road games and a bye week, Lions fans should be going crazy for them on Sunday afternoon. The Green Bay Packers have had a wild up-and-down season so far in 2026. Injuries and off-the-field concerns dropped the team to 1-2 after Week 3. Since then, the team is on a three-game winning streak and heads to Detroit with star running back Josh Jacobs back on the field to give the offense a much-needed boost. While this is Detroit’s first divisional game, the Packers are 1-1 in divisional play this season. Let’s take a deep look at the Packers’ season so far ahead of Week 7. Green Bay Packers 2026 season thus far (4-2) Week 1: Lost to Minnesota Vikings, 39-22 Week 2: Defeated New York Jets, 20-17 (OT) Week 3: Lost to Atlanta Falcons, 35-14 Week 4: Defeated Tampa Bay Buccaneers, 17-14 Week 5: Defeated Chicago Bears, 31-7 Week 6: Defeated Dallas Cowboys, 23-13 Offensive stats: The offense has had a more chaotic ride than the defense. At quarterback, Jordan Love has been doing well, throwing for 1,684 yards with 11 touchdowns and four interceptions. He’s had to carry the offense while the running game has struggled. Love has the third-most passing yards in the NFL, but the passing game hasn’t been all flowers and roses, as it ranks in the middle of the pack in DVOA and PFF. With Jacobs returning, expect that part of the offense to take a step forward. MarShawn Lloyd leads the team with 122 yards and two touchdowns, averaging 2.5 yards per carry. The trade for Kaleb Johnson hasn’t worked out as well as fans hoped, with Johnson getting only 104 yards on 3.7 yards per carry. The running game is the offense’s biggest weakness, ranking in the bottom four in multiple categories, from rushing yards to DVOA to PFF grades. When Love has time to throw, he most often finds wide receivers Christian Watson and Matthew Golden. Watson leads the team in yards (538) and touchdowns (6), while Golden leads in catches with 30. The duo has already combined for over 1,000 yards this season, and they could be the passing game’s future one-two punch if wide receiver Jayden Reed can’t return from his neck injury. Newly paid tight end Tucker Kraft has had a slow start, catching 25 passes for 249 yards and a touchdown. Green Bay’s biggest flaw right now is drops, as they lead the NFL with 20, according to Pro Football Reference. One major reason for the running game’s struggles is the offensive line. Injuries have plagued the position group, and the team has made multiple moves, including signing former Detroit Lion Kevin Zeitler to provide immediate help, although he has yet to play. According to PFF, they have the second-worst run-blocking grade (47.8), but it gets worse. They also have the worst pass-blocking grade from PFF (46.8), which explains why, despite Love’s high mark in passing yards, the passing grades and DVOA aren’t high, but they’re enough to carry the offense and make them an average team in EPA. Defensive stats: The Packers defense has been on the calmer side this year, but not in the front seven. Two defensive tackles and a linebacker are on IR, while their star pass rusher and another defensive tackle are still on PUP. EDGE Lukas Van Ness leads the line with 3.5 sacks, while defensive tackle Devonte Wyatt has 2.0 sacks and a forced fumble as the defense tries to hold down the fort until EDGE Micah Parsons returns. The linebacker room lost its best player, Edgerrin Cooper, for the year with a torn Achilles, but Zaire Franklin and Ty’Ron Hopper are doing their best to keep the defense tough. Franklin has 41 tackles, a forced fumble, and a pass deflection, while Hopper has 12 tackles, two pass deflections, and an interception. Green Bay’s secondary has been the strength of the defense, mostly because of the lack of injuries at the position. Safety Xavier McKinney is back to his old tricks, tied for the league lead with three interceptions, and with Evan Williams next to him with two, this safety duo looks like one of the best in the NFL. With a stout secondary, they rank highly in passing defense in DVOA and passing yards allowed, and PFF rates them the NFL’s top coverage unit. While the passing defense has been stellar, this team is struggling to stop the run, which makes sense with how many bodies are out in that front seven, especially on the interior. With the Packers allowing over 110 rushing yards a game, Detroit may try to use the running game to open up the passing game. Injury notes Key players ruled out : RT Zach Bako-Bewele (IR), LB Edgerrin Cooper (IR), WR Jayden Reed (IR), DT Javon Hargrave (IR), DT Jonathan Ford (IR), WR Skyy Moore (IR) Key players to monitor : TE Luke Musgrave (PUP), EDGE Micah Parsons (PUP), DT Jordon Riley (PUP), G Aaron Banks (knee/toe), T Anthony Belton (knee), C/G Jager Burton (back), C/G Jacob Monk (quad), CB Benjamin St-Juste (hamstring) We thought the Carolina Panthers were banged up. Oh man, the Packers blew them out of the water. Their offensive line took a big blow when they lost their top player, right tackle Zach Bako-Bewele, to a patellar tendon tear that ended his season. Several of these injuries are season-ending, but the Packers are dealing with even more issues. Their superstar Parsons is still on PUP, and he won’t be returning to practice this week, but he’ll be on the field soon enough. Another player still on PUP is tight end Luke Musgrave, as the Packers could use all the help they can get on offense. Last week, the Packers added more players to their IR list: defensive tackles Javon Hargrave and Jonathan Ford, and wide receiver Skyy Moore. Additionally, the offensive line has four linemen (two starters) dealing with issues: left guard Aaron Banks is battling knee and toe issues, and the replacement for Bako-Bewele, Anthony Belton, is dealing with a knee injury. Banks missed Week 6, so his Week 7 status is up in the air. Their depth at guard and center has been rough, too: backup interior lineman Jager Burton missed Week 6 with a back injury, and Jacob Monk is dealing with a quad injury. Cornerback took a little bit of a hit, down Benjamin St-Juste, but it’s nowhere near as depleted as the trenches. Biggest strength: Secondary With injuries depleting the front seven, the secondary is taking on the burden of carrying the defense. They’ve allowed the third-fewest yards per passing attempt. Green Bay leads the NFL in interceptions with nine. When you not only limit what offenses can do through the air but also take away the football, you start changing how offenses attack you. Evan Williams Picks Off Dak Prescott, What A Great Play From The Packers. The Packers Secondary Comes Up With A Huge Interception Right There. Big Time. 🔥 pic.twitter.com/r1qvGb4Es5 — SM Highlights (@SMHighlights1) October 19, 2026 The Packers have allowed the third-lowest passer rating (73.9) and only nine passing plays over 20+ yards, tied for second-fewest in the league. We’ve seen what great safety play is like in Detroit when safeties Kerby Joseph and Brian Branch are on the field together, and the Packers are doing the same with McKinney and Williams. The cornerback room isn’t too impressive, but they’ve done their job well, so with the overtop help being as dominant as it has been, the cornerbacks have more opportunities to make plays and do their part. Biggest weakness: Running back Despite Jacobs returning this week for Green Bay, this position has been a huge problem for them this year. It’s uncertain how ready Jacobs will be and how much he’ll play,…

title: Detroit Lions kick off Packers week with full attendance at practice
summary: The Detroit Lions will have their first division game of the season this Sunday, hosting the 4-2 Green Bay Packers at Ford Field for a 4:25 p.m. ET kickoff. Detroit got a head start on the week, moving their first practice from Wednesday to Tuesday, a common practice from this regime out of a bye […]
full_text: Detroit Lions quarterback Jared Goff (16), offensive lineman Juice Scruggs (70), left, and center Seth McLaughlin (65), quarterback Luke Altmyer (2) practice during training camp at Meijer Performance Center in Allen Park on Monday August 17, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The Detroit Lions will have their first division game of the season this Sunday, hosting the 4-2 Green Bay Packers at Ford Field for a 4:25 p.m. ET kickoff. Detroit got a head start on the week, moving their first practice from Wednesday to Tuesday, a common practice from this regime out of a bye week. According to coach Dan Campbell, it also served the purpose of giving returning players Brian Branch and Cade Mays a big load of work, then giving them—and the rest of the team—Wednesday off to let their bodies recover. “That’s one of the reasons why we’re practicing tomorrow and not Wednesday,” Campbell said Monday. “So, we can push some of these guys a little bit knowing they’re going into a day off. I think that’ll help a little bit.” And if Tuesday’s practice is any indication, the Lions will be entering this pivotal Week 7 matchup with a good bill of health. Not only will Branch and Mays make their 2026 debuts for the team, but Detroit’s Tuesday practice had every single player on the active roster practicing. That includes the return of reserve cornerback Rock Ya-Sin, who had missed last game with a hamstring injury. Now, it wouldn’t be completely accurate to call the Lions “fully healthy” at this point in the season. Just last week, the Lions placed three players—WR Tom Kennedy, G Ben Bartch, and LB Devin White—on injured reserve , with Kennedy out for the season and White out for at least a couple of months with a broken forearm. Beyond that, the Lions still have Isiah Pacheco, Kendrick Law, Avonte Maddox, and Thomas Harper on injured reserve as well. Still, thus far, the Lions’ injury luck has certainly been better than in previous years, and they’ll need all hands on deck for a surging Packers team this week and an undefeated Vikings squad waiting in Week 8. We’ll have a more thorough injury report on Wednesday, when the Lions are expected to drop their first official practice designations of the week.

title: NFL Week 7 power rankings: Are the Detroit Lions a top-10 team?
summary: For many NFL teams, a bye week offers a chance to rest, recover, and reset their focus as they push through the rest of the season. It also creates a mixed bag of perspectives on where they stand relative to the rest of the League. For example, the Detroit Lions entered their Week 6 bye […]
full_text: Oct 11, 2026; Glendale, Arizona, USA; Detroit Lions head coach Dan Campbell against the Arizona Cardinals at State Farm Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Mark J. Rebilas-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect For many NFL teams, a bye week offers a chance to rest, recover, and reset their focus as they push through the rest of the season. It also creates a mixed bag of perspectives on where they stand relative to the rest of the League. For example, the Detroit Lions entered their Week 6 bye in second place in the NFC North, yet they open Week 7 in fourth place, as the Minnesota Vikings were also on a bye and the Chicago Bears and Green Bay Packers each won last Sunday, vaulting them ahead of Detroit in the standings. From a national perspective, that was enough for a few analysts to drop the Lions a spot in their power rankings. However, other national analysts moved the Lions up in their rankings, as other NFL teams—outside the NFC North—have lost some of their luster. Let’s take a closer look at this week’s national power rankings. The Athletic: 9 (Previous rank: 12) From Chad Graff and Josh Kendall : Fantasy focus: Jared Goff Lions running back Jahmyr Gibbs is the low-hanging fruit. He’s leading all fantasy scorers with 30.7 points per game, but that was expected. How about Goff, who is third among quarterbacks in scoring (23.0 ppg)? The 11-year veteran has 12 touchdowns and no interceptions and is fourth in EPA per dropback (0.29). Sports Illustrated: 11 ( Previous rank: 11) From Connor Orr : The Packers and Vikings are next on Detroit’s post-bye schedule. We’ll find out immediately if the defense was fixed, has the potential to be fixed, or if Jared Goff is going to continue needing to score 30-plus a week to keep the Lions in the conversation. USA Today: 11 (Previous rank: 12) From Nate Davis : Still 3-2 after their bye week, they’ve fallen into the NFC North basement … but that can change fast with the Packers and Vikings coming to Ford Field the next two weeks. CBS Sports: 11 (Previous rank: 12) From Pete Prisco : The bye last week was a good thing for an ailing team as they ready to face the hot Packers this week. The key is improving the bad defense going forward. Yahoo Sports: 11 (Previous rank: 13) From Frank Schwab : The Lions’ bye was well timed. The next two weeks they host the Packers and Vikings. Those two games will determine if they’re a factor in a tough NFC North race. They are also getting reinforcements. Center Cade Mays and safety Brian Branch are expected to return from injuries. The Branch return is very interesting for a defense that needs help, though Branch can’t be guaranteed to solve all problems as he comes off a torn Achilles. When healthy, Branch is a difference maker. It remains to be seen if the injury cost him any explosiveness. He won’t get a full snap share right away, Lions head coach Dan Campbell said Monday. But just having him and Mays back gives the Lions hope that they can make a statement in the division race over the next two games. NFL.com: 12 (Previous rank: 11) From Nick Shook : The Lions did nothing to deserve a one-place drop — they had a bye week, after all. Chicago’s upward movement prompted the change. Jared Goff is quietly compiling an incredibly efficient season, and the defense finally stepped up in Detroit’s lopsided Week 5 win over Arizona. Wise individuals know not to overlook the Lions. ESPN: 12 (Previous rank: 11) From ESPN Staff, excerpt from Eric Woodyard : Biggest issue on offense: Third-down conversions Detroit’s offense is tied with Buffalo for the most offensive points scored per game (32.8), which has been fueled by a strong start from veteran QB Jared Goff (12 touchdown passes with zero interceptions). But the Lions could improve on third down. They are currently ranked 22nd in third-down conversion percentage at 37.3%. And to go even deeper, Detroit is tied for dead last in third-and-short percentage (third-and-3 or less) at 43.8% Sporting News: 14 (Previous rank: 13) From Vinnie Iyer : The Lions have a strange defensive dichotomy. They led the league with 20 sacks going into their Week 6 bye, but they also had the No. 32 pass defense. Their job is to turn that pressure into better results in the second half of the season.
author: Erik Schlitt

title: Detroit Lions replace veteran nose tackle with rookie on practice squad
summary: The Detroit Lions made a minor but interesting move on their practice squad on Tuesday afternoon. The team announced they have released veteran nose tackle Chris Smith and replaced him with rookie nose tackle Aidan Keanaaina. Smith is a well-respected player within the building, and even got some early reps in training camp and the […]
full_text: Detroit Lions defensive lineman Aidan Keanaaina (60) practices during OTAs at Meijer Performance Center in Allen Park on Thursday, June 11, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The Detroit Lions made a minor but interesting move on their practice squad on Tuesday afternoon. The team announced they have released veteran nose tackle Chris Smith and replaced him with rookie nose tackle Aidan Keanaaina. Smith is a well-respected player within the building, and even got some early reps in training camp and the preseason. After Smith’s game against the Bengals in August, Lions coach Dan Campbell heaped praise on the 26-year-old defender. “He just does everything right,” Campbell said. “He does all the little things right. He doesn’t make the same mistake twice. He’s the guy you love to coach because he’s up here all offseason, works his tail off, is always trying to hone his game. He plays disciplined football.” Despite a strong preseason, Smith didn’t make the 53-man roster, and he spent the first six weeks on the practice squad without a call-up. Now an undrafted rookie is taking his roster spot. If the name Aidan Keanaaina sounds familiar, it’s because Detroit initially invested heavily in him as an undrafted rookie. Among Detroit’s UDFA class this year, Keanaaina received the highest amount of contract guarantees with $267,500 . Unfortunately for him, he suffered an injury during training camp that landed him on injured reserve, and he was released with an injury settlement shortly thereafter . Clearly, the length of that injury settlement has passed, and Keanaaina can now continue his development with Detroit. With the Lions lacking a ton of depth at nose tackle, it’s certainly possible he eventually sees the field this season, but it’ll take some time for him to get back into football shape. With Keanaaina back in Detroit, he joins five other members of the Lions UDFA class on the roster, including EDGE Eric O’Neill (active roster), quarterback Luke Altmyer, tight end Miles Kitselman (who also returned after his injury settlement expired), EDGE Anthony Lucas, and safety Aamaris Brown.
author: Erik Schlitt

title: Detroit’s best things to do, see, and eat before heading to a Lions game
summary: If you are reading this, let me be among the first to say welcome to Detroit. My name is Morgan Cannon, Lead Analysis writer at PrideofDetroit.com, and local Detroiter here to give you a gameday guide that should help make your trip to the D a memorable one. To begin, Detroit is an old city […]
full_text: Photo by Nic Antaya/Getty Images | Getty Images If you are reading this, let me be among the first to say welcome to Detroit. My name is Morgan Cannon, Lead Analysis writer at PrideofDetroit.com, and local Detroiter here to give you a gameday guide that should help make your trip to the D a memorable one. To begin, Detroit is an old city with a ton of history spanning across centuries. Originally founded as a French trading post back in 1701, Detroit has been a fixture during it all. From being the heart of the automotive industry boom, to being a hub of music and culture, Detroit has a story unlike any other city around. And while many will point to the city’s recent renaissance over the last decade-plus, I would argue that Detroit never left. From downtown to the surrounding neighborhoods that all have their own unique feel; whether you like art exhibits, museums, or want to see live music, Detroit has something for you. Places to stay in Detroit Trumbull and Porter Hotel: Situated between Trumbull and Rosa Parks Boulevard, the Trumbull and Porter hotel is just steps away from the Detroit Riverfront and the newly renovated Ralph C. Wilson Centennial Park. If you have little ones, I would highly suggest making the walk down to the river. Beyond that, making the short trip over to Michigan Central Station is also something I would add to the old itenary. Especially if anyone in your group has an affinity for history and architecture. Detroit Foundation Hotel: Originally the city’s firehouse headquarters, the Detroit Foundation Hotel is one of many buildings that makes Detroit an arhitectural destination. Situated downtown, your walk to Ford Field would be a quick 15-minute trip. On the first floor of the building, you can have a drink or enjoy a meal in The Apparatus Room. Shinola Hotel: If you really want to be in the middle of everything, including for your Lions gameday experience, I would recommend a stay at the Shinola Hotel. Overlooking Woodward avenue, you are within walking distance to everything downtown has to offer, including San Morello on the ground floor. Shinola’s history with Detroit dates back to the early 1900’s, making their presence in the heart of downtown that much cooler. Things to do in Detroit Detroit Institute of Arts: Affectionately referred to as, “The DIA,” by locals, the Detroit Institute of Arts is a must-see for anybody that is interested in art or history. Located in Detroit’s cultural corridor, the building itself is beautiful and the exhibitions are always world-class. Whether you are taking a guided tour through the floors of art, or you are taking in a performance in the theater—the DIA is one thing to check off of your Detroit bucket list. Charles H. Wright Museum of African American History: Not far from the DIA on the campus of Wayne State University is another world class museum that many refer to as, “The Wright.” Depending on the day, there can be programs designed for the youth, live performances, and much more. Eastern Market: The largest outdoor outdoor market district in the country, Eastern Market is one of my favorite areas in the entire city. If you are lucky enough to be visiting the city on a weekend, be sure to get to the market in the morning if you can. Grab a coffee from Mitsos (maybe a morning gyro if you get down like that), walk through the sheds and take in all of the fresh produce, grab a beer at Eastern Market Brewery or Lagerhaus. And if you are into vintage clothes, pop into Wabisabi. On top of the food, Eastern Market is home to a special collection of murals that adorn buildings throughout the district. Best places to eat in Detroit Mitsos Greek Food and Coffee: If you are looking for the best gyro in town, you have to head to Mitsos. It is family-owned and ran, and the owners know all of their regulars by name. From their excellent Freddo coffees, to the fried feta, you simply can’t go wrong when eating at Mitsos. Located in the heart of Eastern Market, you may smell their food before you can even see their spot on Riopelle. La Jalisciense Supermercado Y Taquería: Located on Vernor in Southwest Detroit, La Jalisciense is another family-owned spot that has been serving their community for over a decade. They serve authentic mexican food, and also run a grocery store in the same building. Order some food, grab a few cold drinks, walk through the aisles of the store, and before you head out of the neighborhood, make the short trip down the road and pay a visit to the Mexicantown Bakery . You’re welcome in advance. Marrow in the Market: Also located in the historic Eastern Market District, Marrow in the Market should absolutely be a destination during your trip, especially if you have a foodie in the group. Winner of Hour Detroit’s Best Restaurant in 2026, the ambience is as elite as the food is. Great for a drink while taking in views of Detroit’s skyline, or for a dinner date with the family. Ford Field parking, rideshare, and transit options There are parking structures directly next to Ford Field and Comerica Park, but they will come at a cost—both in terms of dollars and time. However, if it is indeed Winter in Detroit and you aren’t a big fan of the cold, this could be the option for you. Just be prepared for it to take a while to leave those parking garages once the game concludes. Unfortunately, we aren’t exactly known for our superb public transportation in Detroit, but there are a few options. If you are staying downtown somewhere, both the People Mover and the QLine are options you can use if you don’t feel like walking. The People Mover is an elevated train line that provides some good views of downtown on its loop, and the QLine is a trolley that can take you from Campus Martius all the way up to New Center. Both options are free, too. Just like any other large city’s downtown, street parking in Detroit can be hit-or-miss in the sense that you could drive around for half-an-hour and not find a spot, especially on gamedays. Applications like ParkWhiz can sometimes be a better option to secure a spot ahead of time rather than waiting until the day of. Tailgating at Ford Field Eastern Market: I am double-dipping a bit here, but Eastern Market is easily one of the best tailgating scenes in the city. Restaurants like Mitsos, Farmer Franks, and Jose’s are all open, but instead of fruits and vegetables, you get a lot of Lions fans. If you are a little chilly on a crisp December morning and walk quickly, you can make it to Ford Field in about 15 minutes. Midtown : If you make your way over to Cass Avenue, you will find parking lots packed with Lions tailgaters. If you are a Lions fan, most people will welcome you with open arms. And if you are a fan of the visiting team, well then you better come bearing gifts. I’m kidding! Unless you are from Wisconsin because then I am serious. Like Eastern Market, let’s call it a 15 minute walk to the cozy confines of Ford Field. Pride Plaza : Located on Brush Street between Ford Field and Comerica Park, the city shuts the street down and turns the area into a great area for families. They have activities for kids like combine activities for young fans to test their skills, beers and cocktails, and food trucks. The Ford Field Experience While Ford Field was built in 2002, its history runs much deeper than that. Rather than demolishing the Historic Hudson’s Warehouse that was originally constructed in the 1920’s, the developers of Ford Field decided to incorporate the existing structure into their design. The result is a warm, cozy setting that aligns harmoniously with the city’s heritage. That is, until kickoff ensues. After that, 65,000 of the Honolulu blue faithful work themselves into a frenzy, creating one of the better homefield advantages in the entire NFL. From a food and drink perspective, they have really stepped their game up over the years. The typical stadium classics are still there, but the local flavor is really where Ford Field…

title: Detroit Lions still expect Kerby Joseph to play this year
summary: While the Detroit Lions are getting one of their Pro Bowl safeties back this week in Brian Branch, the return of the other—Kerby Joseph—remains a bit of a mystery. Joseph has now been sidelined for over a year with a knee injury that has been described as inoperable and chronic. Joseph’s timeline has seemingly been […]
full_text: Detroit Lions safety Kerby Joseph (31) practices during OTAs at Detroit Lions headquarters and training facility in Allen Park on Thursday, May 30, 2024. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co While the Detroit Lions are getting one of their Pro Bowl safeties back this week in Brian Branch , the return of the other—Kerby Joseph—remains a bit of a mystery. Joseph has now been sidelined for over a year with a knee injury that has been described as inoperable and chronic. Joseph’s timeline has seemingly been pushed back at every turn, but Lions coach Dan Campbell may have finally offered a light at the end of the tunnel. When asked if he expects Joseph to play this season, Campbell answered simply: “I do.” Campbell didn’t provide a timeline for Joseph’s return, but did say they are very encouraged with where things currently stand with his progress. “He’s doing well. I’ll leave it at that. He really is,” Campbell said. “He’s doing a good job. I’m not going to give you a timetable, but I’ve been pleased with where he’s at. He’s in a good headspace right now, which is great, because that’s hard. You’re coming off this, you’re wanting to go, and you’re working at it, and at some point, it’s time for football. We all know that and recognize it, but we’ll take it one day at a time.” A few weeks ago, Branch also offered some hope for Branch’s return. “Kerb’s my dawg. We’ve been—we ain’t quitting, man,” Branch said two weeks ago. “Injured, we’ve been in this thing together for, what, 10 months, man? It’s been a long road. We’ve been fighting every day. He gonna be alright. He gonna be back. We’re gonna be back.” Joseph has been back in the building for a few weeks now after taking some time away for a personal issue. He has not spoken with the media since the very beginning of training camp, when he noted that he was “super optimistic” because of all the work he’s put in . We haven’t had a healthy version of both Branch and Joseph on the field really since the 2024 season. But it looks like the Lions are expected to see it happen again at some point before the season is through.

title: Detroit Lions bye week evaluation: Is the team really on the rise?
summary: One of the more interesting comments from Detroit Lions coach Dan Campbell on Monday was his level of optimism at the bye week compared to last year. Even though Detroit had come off a big win over the Tampa Bay Buccaneers to move to 5-2 last year, Campbell said he feels better about this season […]
full_text: Detroit Lions quarterback Jared Goff leads the team onto the field from the tunnel for the first half against the Arizona Cardinals at State Farm Stadium in Glendale, Arizona on Sunday, Oct. 11, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co One of the more interesting comments from Detroit Lions coach Dan Campbell on Monday was his level of optimism at the bye week compared to last year. Even though Detroit had come off a big win over the Tampa Bay Buccaneers to move to 5-2 last year, Campbell said he feels better about this season because of the youth and growth already shown through five games. “In some regards I feel better going into this bye than even I did last year because I know we’re ascending and we’re young and we’re growing and that’s exciting,” Campbell said. “Sometimes you feel like you’re topped off and maybe you’re beginning to deteriorate because of issues worn down, age, whatever it is. “So that’s exciting. I do feel like we’re on the rise here a little bit. We’ve just got to keep getting better. We’ve got to keep testing ourselves. And look, we’re in for the long haul now and it’s really about to get geared up and the competition is about to really raise up another level, and it starts with Green Bay.” But is that optimism actually warranted? Is this team’s future far more bright than the one that finished 9-8 and out of the playoffs last year? On this week’s PODcast, we re-evaluate how the team has played through five games. What have they done well? What have they struggled with? What successes are likely to continue through January, and which struggles could actually improve in the back half of the season? Last year, John Morton led the highest-scoring offense in the league through the first couple months. What is different about this season that could keep the offense efficient throughout the entire year? And what hope is there that the Lions defense can turn things around? In the last portion of the PODcast, we discuss the outlook of the NFC North and the overall NFC, and where the Lions fall in the clutter. title: Film study: Packers’ deep passing attack is a paper tiger
summary: The Detroit Lions (3-2) will take on their first divisional opponent in Week 7 as the Green Bay Packers (4-2) come to Ford Field Sunday afternoon fresh off two big wins. Let’s just get straight to the point and talk about the elephant in the room. All eyes will be on the Lions defense—and particularly […]
full_text: Oct 11, 2026; Glendale, Arizona, USA; Detroit Lions cornerback Keith Abney II (6) against the Arizona Cardinals at State Farm Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Mark J. Rebilas-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The Detroit Lions (3-2) will take on their first divisional opponent in Week 7 as the Green Bay Packers (4-2) come to Ford Field Sunday afternoon fresh off two big wins. Let’s just get straight to the point and talk about the elephant in the room. All eyes will be on the Lions defense—and particularly the secondary—as it takes on the Packers’ passing attack. Headed into Week 6, the Packers boasted the fourth-highest explosive play rate in passing offense while the Lions defense checked in at 17th, despite giving up a league-high 297.4 passing yards per game. Offensive and defensive explosive play rates: The Bills offense is very good pic.twitter.com/Dr7YFUrYSn — Sam Hoppen (@SamHoppen) October 13, 2026 The mission of this film study is to generate a scouting report aimed at diagnosing what patterns and tendencies, if any, the Packers have shown in their deep passing game and what that means for the Lions defense. So I watched all 32 of the Packers’ pass attempts of 20+ air yards and came away with some interesting insights. Packers’ aggression comes overwhelmingly in comfortable game scripts The first and most critical tendency to take note of is that, per NFL Pro , of the 32 passes of 20+ air yards or more attempted this season, only four have come while trailing their opponent. In fact, all four of these passes came in a single game: Week 3 against the Atlanta Falcons. Digging even deeper, two of the four occurred after the two-minute warning in the fourth quarter, when the Packers were down by a score of 35-14. Further, all four pass attempts were incomplete. Okay, but surely this could be misleading, and the Packers have just played with either a tie or lead in many games, much like we say on “Sunday Night Football” against the Dallas Cowboys? Not really. Quarterback Jordan Love has attempted 60 passes this season while the team has been behind in score. I’ll do the math for you. That is only a 6.67% deep pass rate while trailing. Compare that to 16 deep passes attempted while the Packers are playing with the lead on 103 total passing attempts with a lead. That’s 15.5%. Okay, but surely this is just a small sample size trend, right? Not really. To further magnify the situational shift in play calling, the Packers have attempted short passes of under 10 air yards 64 times on 103 pass plays (62.2%) with the lead compared to 44 times on 60 pass plays (73.3%) while trailing. Head coach Matt LaFleur clearly has a tendency toward paradoxical aggression. He tends to take risks when he’s living in advantageous game scripts, but his focus shifts to a low-risk approach when the game script pressure turns up. This creates a perception of the deep passing game being a strength, but the reality is it’s more of a “kill shot” tool, and when it rains, it pours. Compare that to Lions offensive coordinator and Drew Petzing and Jared Goff, who have executed the same number of deep passes of 20+ air yards or more (6) when trailing in score as when leading in score, showing no situational tendency so far in 2026’s early sample size. For the Lions to avoid falling victim in the explosive passing game, the key to winning here is to score early and play with a lead. Packers’ aggression comes overwhelmingly in certain down-and-distances The second critical tendency to take note of is that, per NFL Pro , the Packers rarely throw the deep ball in short-to-medium yards-to-go situations, especially on second down. Of the 32 passes of 20+ air yards or more, they break down in the following downs and distances: first-and-10 (11) third-and-long (7+ yards) (9) second-and-long (7+ yards) (6) third-and-medium/short (0-6 yards) (4) second-and-medium (4-6 yards) (2) second-and-short (0-3 yards) (0) The key insight here is that LaFleur’s play calling tends not to take advantage of “waste” downs, which I would categorize as the second-and-short/medium range to take shots down the field. Of the two deep passes noted in second-and-medium situations, both were against Dallas in Week 6 and were second-and-6s from inside the Dallas 26-yard line. It is interesting that LaFleur likes to take risks predominantly with the lead, but does not feel comfortable taking the same risks in advantageous down-and-distance situations. Packers’ deep ball success is feast or famine The third critical insight in the Packers’ deep passing game is that its success is remarkably feast or famine. Overall, Jordan Love has completed 10-of-32 (31%) deep passes of 20+ air yards. But six of those 10 completions came in a single game: Week 5 against the Chicago Bears, where Love went 6-for-8 on deep passes. In three games, Love did not complete a single deep pass (0-for-3 vs the New York Jets, 0-for-7 vs the Atlanta Falcons, and 0-for-6 vs the Dallas Cowboys). Without the Week 5 explosion week, the Packers are just 4-for-26 (15.8%) on deep passes on the season. So what happened against the Bears? Five of the eight deep passes against Chicago came on first-and-10 situations, four of which were play-action passes. Below is the first. This is a simple two-man fade-out combination route. If the quarterback sees Cover-3, the out is opened under the outside fade. But in this case, the Bears are in Cover-2, where the deep, field-side safety is responsible for the outside fade. The Bears safety is caught with dirty eyes in the backfield and flat-footed, a huge missed execution play leading to the Green Bay touchdown that should not have been so easy. If the Lions rookie Keith Abney gets more snaps at the free safety spot this week, expect the Packers to test his eyes. A key point in the above clip is that the play design is also a simple single read for Jordan Love. On the two-man route concept, it’s not a strenuous progression with both routes to the same side of the field. Similarly, below is another simple single read concept with the core routes all to the field-side of the formation. LaFleur is not asking a lot of Love with either of these concepts. To his credit, Love executes this with great timing and ball placement before Bears’ rookie safety Dillon Theineman (31) can close the gap in the zone. Overall thoughts The Lions’ passing defense has not been great against deep passes this year, giving up 12 completions on 22 attempts. But outside of the Bears game, the Packers are not an unstoppable force in this area either. In addition to the tendencies discussed already, it’s clear that Love has his favorites, with 14-of-32 deep targets going to Matthew Golden and 10-of-32 going to Christian Watson. It will be interesting to see if defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard deploys any similarly unique coverages against the Packers as he did against the Arizona Cardinals . Lastly, Love does not seem to be impacted one way or the other when it comes to handling pressure in his deep passing ability, as he is 4-of-16 while under pressure and 6-of-16 while kept clean. Score early. Play with a lead. Don’t play with dirty eyes.
author: Anthony Balaj

title: Discussion: How should the Detroit Lions handle Cade Mays’ return?
summary: On Monday, Detroit Lions coach Dan Campbell announced the impending return of two key players. Barring some unforeseen setback, starting center Cade Mays and safety Brian Branch will make their 2026 debuts on Sunday afternoon against the Green Bay Packers. For Branch, his return is pretty simple. While it sounds like the Lions will limit […]
full_text: Jun 17, 2026; Detroit, MI, USA; Detroit Lions quarterback Jared Goff (16) gets ready to take a snap from center Cade Mays (64) during the Detroit Lions veteran’s minicamp at the Allen Park Training Facility. Mandatory Credit: Lon Horwedel-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect On Monday, Detroit Lions coach Dan Campbell announced the impending return of two key players. Barring some unforeseen setback, starting center Cade Mays and safety Brian Branch will make their 2026 debuts on Sunday afternoon against the Green Bay Packers. For Branch, his return is pretty simple. While it sounds like the Lions will limit his reps a bit, Campbell seemed confident the Pro Bowl safety can take on a significant role, and his presence will be welcomed in a secondary that has struggled through five games. Mays’ situation is far more complicated. For one, unlike safety, it’s hard to just give a center a situational role to ease him back in. A team wants to keep their center the same throughout the game for a ton of reasons, but none more important than keeping that exchange between center and quarterback consistent. “We’re still back-and-forth on what do we do with him,” Campbell said of Mays. “Do we work him and Juice (Scruggs) in and out? Do we—the center position, it’s a little different than a guard. That’s somebody that’s constantly touching the football.” Making the transition even tougher is the fact that current Lions starting center Juice Scruggs is playing very good football in Mays’ absence. It’s unlikely that Scruggs takes the starting job from Mays, but I’m sure it does bring up thoughts of, “Why mess with something that’s working?” So today’s Question of the Day is: How should the Lions handle Cade Mays’ return? My answer: Let’s establish what the Lions should do once they believe Mays is fully healthy and ready for a full share of snaps. At that point, I don’t think there should be any question that Mays should be the starting center. Scruggs may be playing well, but Mays is better. There’s a reason Mays was a costly free agent, and Scruggs was part of a trade for a starting running back. I don’t think the perception of these players should change based on a five-game sample size that includes a very rough game from Scruggs vs. the Bills. But what’s a good way to ease Mays in this week? Do you actually give him a few drives at center? Do you have him simulate making protection calls from the sideline? Do you get him out there as an extra lineman in some formations? Or do you just relegate him to some special teams snaps to get him on the field, get used to contact, and re-evaluate next week? I’m leaning toward that last option. I really don’t like the idea of rotating Mays in at center for a drive or two or three. It just seems like too much of a risk. Either make him your starting center or find another way to get him out there. The best way to do that is to give him some special teams reps or jumbo package responsibilities, and then make him the starting center in Week 8 against the Vikings’ tough defense. It’s not an ideal spot to throw him in, but I don’t think there is an ideal option out there. What do you think? How would you handle Cade Mays’ return? Share your ideas in the comment section below. title: Jordan Love’s interception against the Cowboys wasn’t his fault
summary: When a receiver doesn’t run to where he’s supposed to, defenders are able to make plays on the football. The Green Bay Packers benefitted from this on Sunday, when Dallas Cowboys receiver CeeDee Lamb slipped on one of his routes, leading to a cornerback Brandon Cisse’s interception. Unless you were paying close attention on Sunday, […]
full_text: (Photo by Michael Reaves/Getty Images) | Getty Images When a receiver doesn’t run to where he’s supposed to, defenders are able to make plays on the football. The Green Bay Packers benefitted from this on Sunday, when Dallas Cowboys receiver CeeDee Lamb slipped on one of his routes, leading to a cornerback Brandon Cisse’s interception. Unless you were paying close attention on Sunday, though, you probably missed that Packers quarterback Jordan Love’s interception was in part to blame on his target running the wrong route, too. pic.twitter.com/nhDw2PTyYQ — Justis Mosqueda (@JuMosq) October 21, 2026 Earlier this week, Green Bay head coach Matt LaFleur confirmed that receiver Matthew Golden was supposed to run a “Lookie” route from the slot, which makes sense considering the motion that the Packers ran, the matchup they got “on” Golden and the outside target to Golden’s side running a mandatory outside release. pic.twitter.com/0EIG64G12T — Justis Mosqueda (@JuMosq) October 21, 2026 What is a Lookie route? Here’s how it’s described in one of the Packers’ playbooks that I have access to. Essentially, a receiver runs vertical, stutters and then his first option on the route is to run a slant. If the defender on him has hard inside leverage on him (square leverage is a slant, as well as outside leverage), then he’s supposed to convert and run an out route. In the book, the receiver is instructed to “make every effort to cross the defender’s face” for a slant. pic.twitter.com/3MBLZK9d0J — Justis Mosqueda (@JuMosq) October 21, 2026 To make it simple: It’s an option route from the slot (slant or out), which is why the outside receiver is instructed to run an “M.O.R.” in the Packers’ playbook. “M.O.R” means a mandatory outside release. Basically, the outside receiver is just there to clear space for the slot, in case an out route does happen. The Lookie route is also the first read on the play. Teams like to call this when they get an advantageous matchup (like a slot receiver on a non-defensive back), as it gives the route-runner a “two-way go” to make that defender wrong 100 percent of the time — at least on paper. Below is the full play from the interception against the Cowboys. pic.twitter.com/09NIxbwx25 — Justis Mosqueda (@JuMosq) October 21, 2026 What’s interesting about this play is the motion, as Golden goes from what was a trips side to what was the single-receiver side. Because the Packers started out in trips and motioned Golden away from the slot, the slot defender couldn’t travel with Golden, forcing an off-ball linebacker to play “on” Golden. (Note: They were in zone, so no one is truly man-to-man.) Golden ends up square with the linebacker after his stutter, but decided to break outside anyway, which gave the linebacker, who had a flat responsibility in quarters coverage, the opportunity to undercut the football. According to LaFleur, Love expected Golden to run the slant, which is why the ball was a little late on the out route. Certainly, Golden didn’t “make every effort to cross the defender’s face” for the slant. LaFleur also mentioned that something happened on the backside of the play to force the Mike linebacker to squeeze the window tighter than expected too (it was the Will linebacker who was “on” Golden), but Christian Watson, who was in the opposite slot, appears to have run a “China” route, which is common on the backside of Lookie plays. I’m not in the coaches’ room and very well could be wrong (and it would not be my first time), but I would assume that the flub was on the running back. Often, these “Lookie” plays are run out of empty (to stretch the spacing of that Mike linebacker), so it’s possible the back wasn’t even supposed to be on the backfield in that play. pic.twitter.com/l2ka8VsxVS — Justis Mosqueda (@JuMosq) October 10, 2023 The Lookie route is very common in the NFL, and the Packers have been on the wrong end of it before. Notably, it’s how then-Raider Davante Adams got an explosive catch-and-run (out of an empty set) when Preston Smith was split out in space (as a flat defender) a couple of years ago. That is what the play was supposed to look like when Green Bay ended up with Golden “on” a linebacker after the motion. Unfortunately, a wrong decision on an option route can disrupt the timing of a pass and put a defender in a position to make a play on the ball. Hopefully, Golden can learn from this lesson and not repeat his mistake.
author: Justis Mosqueda

title: Packers sign former 1st-round defensive tackle Mazi Smith to practice squad
summary: Reinforcements are coming for the Green Bay Packers’ battered defensive line. In week 5, the team lost veteran Javon Hargrave for the season to a torn Achilles tendon, and the team has been dealing with a number of other injuries across the front over the course of this season, including nose tackle Jonathan Ford heading […]
full_text: ARLINGTON, TX - NOVEMBER 10: Mazi Smith #58 of the Dallas Cowboys looks on from the field during an NFL football game against the Philadelphia Eagles at AT&T Stadium on November 10, 2024 in Arlington, Texas. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images Reinforcements are coming for the Green Bay Packers’ battered defensive line. In week 5, the team lost veteran Javon Hargrave for the season to a torn Achilles tendon, and the team has been dealing with a number of other injuries across the front over the course of this season, including nose tackle Jonathan Ford heading to injured reserve last week. As a result, the team’s front office has looked to the free agent market to bolster the team’s depth and has now signed a former high draft pick to the practice squad. That player is Mazi Smith, who was a first-round draft pick by the Dallas Cowboys in 2023. Smith, who measured in at 6-foot-3 and 323 pounds at that year’s NFL Combine, played every game for Dallas over his first two seasons, recording two sacks. However, the Cowboys jettisoned him midway through the 2025 season, sending him to the New York Jets as part of their trade to acquire fellow defensive tackle Quinnen Williams. After being released on cutdown day in August, Smith signed with the Miami Dolphins’ practice squad and was elevated for one game earlier this season, but Miami released him a week ago. Green Bay has now officially signed him to their own practice squad, releasing running back Damon Bankston to clear a spot. Like a certain other former Packers defender who now plays for the Cowboys, Smith was an athletic marvel whose production has yet to live up to his potential. He was a top high school recruit in his home state of Michigan, but he recorded just a half-sack and six tackles for loss over parts of four seasons (two as a full-time player) for the Michigan Wolverines. In Dallas, his struggles against the run — particularly when he became a full-time starter in 2024 — were a driving force behind the Cowboys pushing to add a defensive tackle when they traded away Micah Parsons. That eventually contributed to the Packers being Parsons’ eventual destination when they agreed to send Kenny Clark to Dallas as part of the trade package. For the time being, the Packers have just four defensive tackles on the 53-man roster: Karl Brooks, Devonte Wyatt, Chris McClellan, and Anthony Campbell. Hargrave, Ford, and Warren Brinson are all on injured reserve, while Jordon Riley appears to be getting close to returning to active duty from the PUP list. Smith now joins rookie David Blay, Jr. on the practice squad as the Packers’ depth options at defensive tackle.

title: Packers Film Room: Matthew Golden rights a past wrong
summary: There’s not much that makes me sadder than a cool concept that doesn’t pay off, and Green Bay Packers fans saw this in Week 3. Early in the game, the Packers broke out a slick variant of Hank. Hank is a quick game concept, with the outside man running a Hitch route and the inside […]
full_text: Green Bay Packers wide receiver Matthew Golden (0) is tackled by Dallas Cowboys' Shavon Revel Jr. (28) on a 37-yard reception during the first quarter of their game Sunday, Oct. 18, 2026 at Lambeau Field in Green Bay, Wisconsin. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co There’s not much that makes me sadder than a cool concept that doesn’t pay off, and Green Bay Packers fans saw this in Week 3. Early in the game, the Packers broke out a slick variant of Hank. Hank is a quick game concept, with the outside man running a Hitch route and the inside man running a Flat route. It’s not generally an explosive concept, but it’s been a solid, chain-moving concept for the Packers. On the season, Hank has gained an average of 5.8 YPA and has a success rate of 50%. On this particular version, the receiver who runs the Hitch route is supposed to give a quick cut on the Hitch, then turn upfield on a vertical. It’s a Hitch-and-Go. And, since a Slant-and-Go is called a Sluggo, I’ve been calling this a Huggo. Against the Falcons, Golden is on the Huggo. The play ends with an incomplete pass, with what appears to be a Jordan Love overthrow. It’s a good concept that doesn’t hit. There were a lot of things about that Week 3 game that made me sad, but this was certainly high on the list. Fast forward to this past week: a win against the Cowboys. Midway through the 1st quarter, the Packers tried it again. Once again, Golden is running the Huggo from the outside. There’s some contact as he releases off the line, but he is able to spin cleanly to the outside, away from coverage. This time, it’s a beautiful throw from Jordan Love. He just lays this ball right over Golden’s shoulder, landing as light as a feather. This ended up going for 37 yards. A few plays later, the Packers scored a TD to take a 7-0 lead. We’re not really breaking that down here, but I did want to include it. Golden is on a post and Love is able to hold the safety in place. His feet and shoulders are pointed to the outside, but he opens up on the throw and releases to the middle. The safety is looking for something to his outside shoulder, so the middle is open for Golden. Back to Huggo. Why did it work this week? Was it as simple as the throw being better? We’ve seen this concept a couple times over the years, and the Huggo route was always a pretty quick sell. Quick break on the Hitch then an almost immediate spin in the other direction and a vertical release. Against the Falcons, Golden had a definite stop, sit then spin outside. That’s different than how we had seen it run it in the past. The timing was different. That stop on the Hitch before releasing meant it was longer before Golden was downfield. When I looked at this play in Week 3 , I wondered whether that stop from Golden was a change in the way this was coached, or whether Golden was just taking an extra beat on the route. With what we saw this week, I think we have our answer. Golden cuts on the Hitch then spins and releases quickly. If you look at the videos at the same time, you’ll see that Golden is 4-5 yards downfield against the Cowboys by the time he starts his spin against the Falcons. (Falcons game is on the top, Cowboys on the bottom.) It’s small, but the details matter. They got it nailed down against the Cowboys and it led to a big play. title: Green Bay’s best things to do, see, and eat before heading to a Packers game
summary: Attending a Green Bay Packers game in historic Lambeau Field is on the bucket list of many football fans, and the experience absolutely will live up to the hype. There is not a friendlier fanbase in football (even to visiting Chicago fans!), and the small city charm, beautiful stadium, and unpredictable weather create a truly […]
full_text: Gpg Hunter Hayes Titletown Beats 7162022 0001 | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co Attending a Green Bay Packers game in historic Lambeau Field is on the bucket list of many football fans, and the experience absolutely will live up to the hype. There is not a friendlier fanbase in football (even to visiting Chicago fans!), and the small city charm, beautiful stadium, and unpredictable weather create a truly surreal experience. However, the actual process of visiting Green Bay for a game can be a bit intimidating for outsiders, as there are some trade-offs involved in being the NFL’s smallest market. It can be tricky to find a place to stay, especially without a local’s understanding of the surrounding communities and bar shuttle culture. And while parking is shockingly easy, it can seem odd to find yourself parking in a random person’s backyard. Green Bay is above all a party town in a party state. This guide will get you off on the right foot, but once you are out into the Green Bay wild, my best advice is to ask a random stranger for a recommendation. People from Wisconsin LOVE sharing what they like with out of towners. They DESPERATELY want you to see how amazing their state is and will almost provide an enthusiastic recommendation that you would never find otherwise. Places to stay in Green Bay The single most difficult part of traveling to a Packer game is deciding where to stay, because hotel rooms on game days sell out almost instantly when they become available. If you are lucky enough to find a spot in town, expect to pay handsomely for the privilege, and expect to pay for the entire weekend as most hotels do not permit single-day bookings on game day weekends. The Lodge Kohler is among the fanciest places in all of Green Bay, just yards from Lambeau Field, and features the signature Kohler spa treatments as well. They allegedly sell out for the year as soon as the Packer schedule is posted, but if you’re lucky, and rich enough to score a room here, nothing is more convenient. If you want to be close to the action without paying spa prices, or you have kids in tow, the Quality Inn on Holmgren is also a perfectly fine hotel with good proximity to Lambeau. Either of these options will allow you to walk to all of the major Lambeau-adjacent bars, restaurants, and other downtown amenities. But Green Bay is also not your only choice, and if you haven’t planned months in advance, you will need to get creative. Many people prefer to stay just to the South in Appleton, a fine city in its own right. Appleton offers many fine hotel options and importantly, many bar shuttles that will take you right to the game and bring you right back to the hotel afterwards. It’s a short commute, and the next best thing to staying in Green Bay. Or, if you want to make a weekend out of it, I would highly recommend trucking further North into Door County. Sturgeon Bay and Little Sturgeon are just forty-five minutes from Lambeau and you can often find a cute lakeside cabin via VRBO or Airbnb to take in some nature while not at the game. Some friends and I stayed on the bay side in a cabin for the NFL draft in 2025 and it was an excellent choice, especially considering the traffic into Green Bay is far less severe from the North. In the fall, spending a Saturday in Sister Bay, Egg Harbor, or Ephraim will get you in a nice, relaxed frame of mind for the following day’s game. Things to do in Green Bay Before we get to Green Bay itself, I would recommend anyone driving up to Green Bay from Milwaukee (or Chicago) make a stop at the Greenhouse at the American Club in Kohler. The courtyard at the American Club is one of the most beautiful places in the state, and the Greenhouse is one of the best coffee houses anywhere. They also offer ice cream for the kids, perhaps on the way back home. As previously mentioned, trekking to Door County is a great off-day choice, but Green Bay has plenty to offer as well, including the National Railroad Museum and the Green Bay Botanical Gardens . If you lean to the artsy side, grab some more caffeine at Kompound , and stop by the Art Garage Gallery . But if you’re here for football, you need to make time for the Packer Hall of Fame . Not every team can pull off something like this, but the Packers are so old, and their legacy so deep that the Packer Hall almost feels like a displaced wing of the Pro Football Hall of Fame. It’s truly like stepping into the past. And finally, if you do choose to dine at either of my first two restaurant recommendations (foreshadowing!), you should check out the outdoor offerings of the Titletown District , especially if you have children with you. Ariens Hill is famous for sledding when the snow rolls in, but even in nice weather you will find hundreds of kids running/rolling down it, which they seem to enjoy for some reason. Next to the hill you will find a variety of lawn games like shuffleboard and ping pong, all in the shadows of Lambeau. Green Bay is a fun town, and the general Green Bay/Appleton/Door County has something to offer for everyone, from families, to outdoorsmen, to city folk. Best places to eat in Green Bay Wisconsin loves “BIG” food. I’m not really sure how else to describe a culture that took cheese and decided that it should be deep fried, and also you should absolutely have cheese curds while you’re in town, but you should also have a butter burger, and the place you should get that butter burger is Kroll’s West , just across the street from Lambeau. Kroll’s is a Green Bay institution that began as a bespoke burger joint that also cooks a little bit of everything. The kind of place that serves up pizza, hot ham and rolls, sandwiches, fried items, etc. But the butter burger is the reason to go, along with a true sense of what the general Lambeau Field area once was before all of the recent upgrades and development. Kroll’s sits just outside of the Titletown district and to be fair, they are not completely immune to modernization as their front parking lot now hosts an immense beer garden party complete with a live band before games, but inside, Kroll’s is still Kroll’s. Over in Titletown, my personal favorite is Hinterland , although there are a wide variety of cuisines available within a short walk , so take a look around before you decide. I know craft breweries are a bit passe at this point, but Hinterland has been making quality beer for thirty years, and Luna Coffee Stout remains one of the best stouts in existence, though if you prefer your beer lighter, there is still plenty to like. More than anything, Hinterland’s cuisine is shockingly good, and I would urge you to try the Italian Meat Pizza with Korean Grilled Short Rib appetizer. Everyone from Wisconsin has an opinion on the best Supper Club, and honestly, you can’t really go wrong with ninety percent of Wisconsin Supper Clubs (and if you don’t know what a Supper Club is, well, there’s a Wikipedia page) . Also, you should go to one while you’re here! Club Chalet in Green Bay is quite good, but lamentably closed on Sundays, so you’ll need to make it part of your pregame schedule. If you want to hit up a supper club post-game, I recommend heading twenty minutes west to nearby Seymour Wisconsin, and the Hotel Seymour Supper Club . Whichever you choose, get yourself a nice steak, don’t fill up on the relish tray, and make sure to leave room for a Brandy Alexander for dessert. And generally speaking, supper clubs make the best Wisconsin Old Fashioneds, so if you haven’t ordered one yet, now is the time. As a warning, You may need some time to decompress afterwards. Lambeau Field parking, rideshare, and transit options While staying in Green Bay can be tricky, parking for a Packer game is almost comically easy, especially if you show up early to take in Titletown or do some tailgating. Even if you are able to acquire a parking pass for the Lambeau Field parking lot, I would recommend forgoing this option and instead engaging in the…

summary: In this space, we look at the snap-to-hold operation on field goals and extra points. We’ve got 5 we’re looking at this week. Trey Smack made all 5 kicks (2 extra points, 3 field goals), but how did the operation look? Let’s start with the snap location for the holder, Daniel Whelan: Kick 1: Extra […]
full_text: GREEN BAY, WISCONSIN - NOVEMBER 28: Long snapper Matt Orzech #42 of the Green Bay Packers warms up prior to an NFL game against the Miami Dolphins at Lambeau Field on November 28, 2024 in Green Bay, Wisconsin. (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images In this space, we look at the snap-to-hold operation on field goals and extra points. We’ve got 5 we’re looking at this week. Trey Smack made all 5 kicks (2 extra points, 3 field goals), but how did the operation look? Let’s start with the snap location for the holder, Daniel Whelan: Kick 1: Extra Point (Made) Snap up and to the body of Whelan, rotation has the laces pointed in. Nice easy catch, hold and spin for Whelan and a clean kick by Smack. Kick 2: 25 yard Field Goal (Made) Snap is right in the sweet spot: up and over the hold point. Whelan makes the catch with his fingers on the laces. Good spin and hold, with the ball leaning slightly forward and away from Smack. Clean kick, splitting the uprights. Kick 3: Extra Point (Made) Good snap from Orzech, over the hold point. It looks like Whelan catches the back of the ball, so there’s a slight hiccup in the hold, but nothing Whelan can’t recover from. He gets the hold down and Smack splits the uprights. Kick 4: 44 yard Field Goal (Made) The snap is slightly higher than the last one, but it’s over the hold point. Whelan catches this one by the laces. Good hold and Smack knocks it though. Kick 5: 29 yard Field Goal (Made) Snap is up and into the body of Whelan. Whelan catches it by the laces, good hold, good kick. With the exception of the slight hiccup from Whelan on Kick 3 (which did not impact the overall timing of the process), this is the cleanest game we’ve seen from this operation in a game this year. Good game. Albums listened to: The Avalanches – No Bad Memories

title: Green Bay Packers News: Packers battling penalty onslaught
summary: I’m of two minds when it comes to talking about the refs and penalties and everything that goes into officiating a professional football game. On the one hand, officiating an NFL game is a massively complex undertaking. Have you read the NFL rulebook? Have you tried? A page turner it is not. The section for […]
full_text: JACKSONVILLE, FL - DECEMBER 14: A yellow penalty flag is picked during the game at Jacksonville Municipal stadium on December 14, 2008 in Jacksonville, Florida. (Photo by Sam Greenwood/Getty Images) | Getty Images I’m of two minds when it comes to talking about the refs and penalties and everything that goes into officiating a professional football game. On the one hand, officiating an NFL game is a massively complex undertaking. Have you read the NFL rulebook? Have you tried? A page turner it is not. The section for roughing the passer alone is 950 words. I know this for a fact because I checked after Sunday night’s impromptu roughing the passer festival, and now I’m actually surprised it isn’t called more considering the broad leeway officials have. It’s genuinely hard to know what to call and what not to call. But on the other hand, shouldn’t it be…I don’t know…better than this? Every game is a flag fest and every play takes place under a looming yellow specter. Did a cool thing just happen? Better hold your breath until you see whether or not there’s laundry on the field. You never know when the capricious gaze of black-and-white striped justice will turn your way. I know there’s plenty of data out there about the increase of penalties, but if you’ll allow me to get a little more squishy about it than just looking at the numbers, it feels bad out there. The vibe, as they say, is off. There’s little reason to assume any game you watch is going to unfold without at least one or two completely arbitrary penalties. Discussing any game inevitably hinges on what penalties were or were not called. It’s not a fun way to watch a game! And I don’t know how you fix it. The genie is out of the bottle, in a sense, because you can’t just go back to not throwing as many flags. We’ve already seen what draws a penalty and what doesn’t. Walking it back now is just setting a different paradigm. That might be the only way, though. If nothing’s getting called, everything could feel less arbitrary. That’s small comfort in an NFL landscape increasingly ruled by seemingly random flags. title: Houston’s best things to do, see, and eat before heading to a Texans game
summary: Houston doesn’t get the same kind of tourist attention that other major cities in this country get. Think about it for a moment, when you think of New York you think Statue of Liberty and the Empire State Building; Los Angeles has Hollywood and…um…other stuff, I’m sure. But when you think of Houston, you don’t […]
full_text: HOUSTON, TX- SEPTEMBER 13: Houston Texans fans tailgate before the Texans play the Kansas City Chiefs in a NFL game on September 13 2015 at NRG Stadium in Houston, Texas. (Photo by Bob Levey/Getty Images) | Getty Images Houston doesn’t get the same kind of tourist attention that other major cities in this country get. Think about it for a moment, when you think of New York you think Statue of Liberty and the Empire State Building; Los Angeles has Hollywood and…um…other stuff, I’m sure. But when you think of Houston, you don’t have that automatic first tourist thought. So most tourists don’t make it their first choice for a destination. Good. That just means for those of you who do travel to Houston for a Texans game, there’s so much to discover and love about the only city in Texas that matters. Because Houston is a truly fascinating place. And those who make the effort to explore the fourth largest city in the country are in for a great time. Because there’s something for everybody in Houston. It’s a vast city with diverse interests, cultures, and ideas and I would bet money which I don’t have that when you come to Houston, you will find something to love about it. The only regret I have about writing this guide is that I can’t list all of the attractions and restaurants that Houston has to offer; so I offer instead a starter’s pack for things to do when you’re not going to a Texans game. Places to stay in Houston First, let’s start with places to stay in Houston. Ideally, you’ll want to be close to the stadium, but that’s not always possible. If you can, the Wyndham Houston is walking distance to Reliant Stadium. Looking for something a little larger and more family-friendly (not that the Wyndham isn’t, I just needed a transitional phrase here), the Doubletree Hilton in the Galleria is on the west end of town by the largest mall in the city. So when you aren’t checking Houston out, you can stroll through the Galleria and window shop. If money truly is no object to you, first of all I’m jealous, and second, the place you want to go is the Post Oak Hotel which is also near the Galleria and the only five-star luxury hotel in the city built by Houston Rockets owner (among other things) Tillman Fertitta. If you have money to burn, they have an incinerator waiting for you. Things to do in Houston Houston is Space City. Never mind what Orlando would have you believe. It’s home to NASA’s Space Center Houston , which is one of the largest STEM learning centers in the country. It is the home to countless artifacts from previous lunar missions like lunar regolith (moonrocks and moondust), spacesuits, mission flight simulators, and so much more. It’s a great way to spend an afternoon in H-Town. For those of you who want to take in some culture while you’re in town, the Menil Collection is for you. It’s a 30-acre campus set in a residential neighborhood just north of the Museum District (also a good time), and has one of the largest collection of surrealists paintings in the country and the single largest collection of Rene Magritte’s work outside of his native Belgium. But we can’t forget to find someplace fun for the kids to unwind. For that, your best bet is to go to the Kemah Boardwalk . Located on Galveston Bay, Houston’s outlet into the Gulf of Mexico, it has roller coasters, zip lines, carnival games, a stingray pond, and several dining options to please every palate. Best places to eat in Houston Houston has one of the most diverse populations in the country, and that is one of the city’s greatest strengths. Why? Because no matter what kind of cuisine you are looking for, Houston almost certainly has it. It’s best known, obviously, for its barbecue shops, Tex-Mex (and classical Mexican too), and Cajun food. But if you don’t feel like eating the specialties of the town, there are other options for you. If you’re looking for a place that’s family friendly or an attraction that’s fun for kids, you can kill two birds with one stone at the Downtown Aquarium . It’s a fun day out with the family with a restaurant (I cannot confirm one way or another whether you should get the seafood there). If you’re looking for something a little more formal and classy (like me), Brennan’s is a can’t-miss. Brennan’s is a Houston institution that’s been around since 1967 and serves Cajun classics and original Cajun-influenced creations. And of course, no restaurant guide, not even one as short as this, is complete without mentioning Mama Ninfa’s on Navigation . This is where tacos al carbon (fajitas) were born, at least according to them. It’s a fun, festive environment with all the authentic Tex-Mex staples you know and love. If you can’t make it to Mama Ninfa’s, El Tiempo Cantina is a great option, and fun fact: El Tiempo was founded by one of Mama Ninfa’s sons, Roland Laurenzo. Word of advice: If you go to El Tiempo, the margaritas are delicious and STRONG. Consider yourself warned. Reliant Stadium parking, rideshare, and transit options One of the things about Houston is that it’s big. Really big. I don’t mean just because it’s the fourth largest city in the country, but the city itself is enormous. Houston is known for its urban sprawl. With that in mind, I am going to level with y’all and say your best bet for enjoying a Texans game is to drive to the stadium. Parking passes are available for purchase on Ticketmaster and it’s going to make your life so much easier (if you have a car or have rented one) to just drive to the game yourself. If you do, the fine folks at Reliant Stadium have a page on their website that shows you how to navigate the various stadium lots, how long the lines are at each gate, and how long the lines are to get into the stadium itself. The stadium opens four hours before kickoff, but in order to avoid the longest lines, I recommend you arrive at least an hour and a half before kickoff. After that, the roads become jammed and a nightmare to navigate. If you do not have a car or don’t feel like renting one, Metro does have park and ride options and a light rail to get to the stadium. Your best bet would be to take one of the various park and ride lots to the light rail, which goes directly to Reliant Stadium. It’s a complicated mess, but it’ll save you a lot of money on cars and parking passes. There is also a rideshare drop off point in front of the yellow lot on Main Street, but unless you are staying (or live) pretty close to the stadium, this is going to cost you a fortune. It can be done, mind you, but I wouldn’t recommend it. Tailgating at Reliant Stadium Texans fans take their tailgating seriously. But they’re also incredibly friendly people who will adopt you as their own if you bring along something to contribute to tailgates. It doesn’t have to be much, bring some brats or soda or even paper plates, and you’ll be welcomed with open arms. The lots open four hours prior to kickoff (except for the platinum lot which opens five hours before kickoff) so if you really want to take in the tailgate experience, to smell the cooking meats, the blasting of chopped and screwed hip hop or unchopped and unscrewed country music in the air, watch fans toss the football around, you can wander to your heart’s content. If you want to take in the tailgating experience, without all that fuss of buying a ticket to the Texans game, they do sell tailgate-only tickets which will allow you to roam the tailgates and, presumably, find a party to watch the game with. There are so many options for tailgating, but a favorite of mine is Lone Spot Tailgaters , who are very welcoming, have foods and spirits that you might not encounter anywhere else other than Houston (well, maybe other parts of Texas, but we don’t care about those right now). They can be found in the Platinum Lot very close to the stadium itself. If you don’t feel like going through the tailgates, there is also the Bud Light Plaza experience where you can listen to live music, get autographs from…
